cards.title: Input GST (Input Tax Credit, ITC) is the GST paid on purchases of goods or…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Input GST (Input Tax Credit, ITC) is the GST paid on purchases of goods or services that are used for business purposes and are eligible for credit under the GST law. Output GST is the GST collected on sales of goods or services. For intra‑state supplies the tax splits into CGST (Central GST) and SGST (State GST); for inter‑state supplies it is IGST (Integrated GST). The net GST payable by a registered person is calculated as Output GST – Input GST for each tax head, subject to the set‑off hierarchy: IGST credit is first used to pay IGST, then CGST, then SGST; CGST credit pays CGST then IGST; SGST credit pays SGST then IGST. If input credit exceeds output liability, the excess may be carried forward or claimed as refund as per rules. This mechanism avoids cascading tax and ensures tax is paid only on value addition.
steps: Input GST is a credit you earn by paying tax on business purchases, and output GST is the tax you collect on sales, with the government only requiring the net tax on value added.

Output GST is a liability because it is collected from customers on behalf of the government.
The set-off hierarchy is mandatory: IGST credit is the most flexible, while CGST and SGST credits are restricted to their own heads and IGST.
Value addition is the core principle; by subtracting input tax from output tax, the system ensures tax is only paid on the profit or value added by the business.

cards.title: GST computation problems require the student to calculate the tax components…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: GST computation problems require the student to calculate the tax components — CGST, SGST, and IGST — for a given taxable value and applicable GST rate, and then determine the net tax liability after adjusting input tax credit. In an intra‑state supply, the GST rate is split equally into CGST (central) and SGST (state); each equals half the GST rate applied to the taxable value. In an inter‑state supply, the full GST rate is levied as IGST (integrated) on the taxable value. Input GST is the tax paid on purchases (CGST, SGST, or IGST depending on the nature of the purchase). Output GST is the tax collected on sales (again CGST, SGST, or IGST). The net GST payable for each component is Output GST minus Input GST of the same component; any excess credit is carried forward. The relationships are: - CGST = SGST = (GST Rate / 2) × Taxable Value (intra‑state) - IGST = GST Rate × Taxable Value (inter‑state) - Net CGST Payable = Output CGST – Input CGST (if positive) - Net SGST Payable = Output SGST – Input SGST (if positive) - Net IGST Payable = Output IGST – Input IGST (if positive) All amounts are expressed in Indian Rupees (₹). The problems test the ability to identify the transaction type, apply the correct split, compute each component, and perform the credit adjustment.

IGST = full GST rate for inter‑state.

cards.title: GST on imports is levied under the Integrated GST (IGST) Act on the assessable…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: GST on imports is levied under the Integrated GST (IGST) Act on the assessable value of the goods plus any customs duty paid. The formula is IGST = (Assessable Value + Customs Duty) × applicable GST rate. This treats an import as an inter‑state supply, ensuring both central and state revenues are captured in a single tax. Exports are classified as zero‑rated supplies under Section 16 of the IGST Act: the GST rate on the export invoice is 0 %, but the exporter is entitled to claim input tax credit (ITC) for all GST paid on inputs, input services, and capital goods used in making the exported product. The ITC can be utilised to offset other tax liabilities or claimed as a refund. The relationship between the two concepts is that both rely on the IGST framework — imports attract IGST at the border, while exports enjoy a zero rate with full credit continuity. This maintains the destination‑based consumption principle: tax accrues where goods are consumed (imports) and is removed where goods leave the tax territory (exports).

cards.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a single…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a single, destination‑based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services in India. It subsumes multiple central and state taxes. For intra‑state supplies the tax is split equally into Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST), each at half the applicable rate. For inter‑state supplies a single Integrated GST (IGST) equal to the full rate is charged. Every registered dealer collects output GST on sales and claims input GST credit on purchases. The net GST payable to the government is Output GST minus eligible Input GST credit. The tax base is the transaction value (taxable value) which includes all duties, charges and expenses incidental to the supply but excludes GST itself. Rates are notified in four slabs: 5 %, 12 %, 18 % and 28 %. The computation follows: CGST = (Rate/2) % × Taxable Value SGST = (Rate/2) % × Taxable Value IGST = Rate % × Taxable Value Net GST Payable = Output GST – Input GST Credit (subject to utilisation rules: IGST credit first offsets IGST, then CGST, then SGST).
steps: The net GST payable is determined by the difference between the tax collected on sales (Output GST) and the tax paid on purchases (Input GST), following a specific hierarchy for credit utilisation.
Intra-state transactions (same state) require splitting the GST rate equally between CGST and SGST.
Inter-state transactions (different states) require the full GST rate to be charged as IGST.
The credit utilisation hierarchy is mandatory: IGST credit must first settle IGST liability, then CGST, then SGST;
CGST credit settles CGST only;
SGST credit settles SGST only.

cards.title: The Banking chapter in ICSE Class 10 Commercial Mathematics introduces the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Banking chapter in ICSE Class 10 Commercial Mathematics introduces the Recurring Deposit (RD) account, a systematic savings instrument where a fixed sum is deposited every month for a predetermined period. The chapter covers three tightly linked sub-concepts: 1. Recurring Deposit Accounts – definition, features (monthly instalment, tenure, rate of interest), and how they differ from fixed deposits and savings accounts. 2. Maturity Value Formula – the algebraic expression M = P × n + P × (n(n+1))/(2) × (r)/(12 × 100) that yields the total amount payable at the end of the term, where P is the monthly instalment, n the number of months, and r the annual rate of interest. 3. Interest Computation for RD – derivation of the interest component I = P × (n(n+1))/(2) × (r)/(12 × 100) from the principle of simple interest on each monthly deposit for the remaining months. These ideas build on the simple-interest formula SI = (P × R × T)/(100) learned in earlier classes and extend it to a series of cash-flows. Mastery enables students to evaluate savings schemes, compare bank offers, and solve ICSE-style word problems that test both algebraic manipulation and financial reasoning.
steps: A Recurring Deposit is essentially a series of small, individual simple-interest loans stacked together over time.

The primary takeaway is that because each monthly instalment remains in the bank for a different duration, the total interest is the sum of interest earned on each individual deposit, which results in a triangular…
Supporting arguments:
Each deposit has a unique holding period: the first instalment earns interest for the full tenure, while the final instalment earns interest for only one month.
The sum of these varying time periods creates the triangular number factor (n(n+1))/(2), which is central to the RD interest formula.
Comparing different bank schemes requires calculating the maturity value for each, as variations in tenure and interest rates significantly impact the final payout.

cards.title: A recurring deposit (RD) account is a time‑bound savings scheme offered by…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A recurring deposit (RD) account is a time‑bound savings scheme offered by banks where a depositor commits to deposit a fixed amount (the monthly installment, denoted P) at regular monthly intervals for a predetermined tenure n (in months). Each installment is treated as a separate principal that earns simple interest at the annual rate r % for the remaining period until maturity. The maturity value M is the sum of all installments (total principal = P × n) plus the aggregate interest earned on each installment. Key sub‑concepts: (i) Installment regularity – missing a payment may attract penalty; (ii) Interest calculation – interest on the k‑th installment is computed for (n‑k+1) months; (iii) Maturity – the account closes after the n‑th installment and the bank pays the maturity value. The RD differs from a fixed deposit where a lump sum is placed at once, and from a savings account where withdrawals are flexible.

You want to save for 2 years, i.e., n = 24 months.

cards.title: The maturity value (M) of a recurring deposit (RD) account is the sum of all…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The maturity value (M) of a recurring deposit (RD) account is the sum of all monthly instalments (P) paid over n months plus the simple interest earned on each instalment for the period it remains in the account. In a CISCE ICSE Class 10 context, interest is calculated at a fixed annual rate r % per annum, compounded quarterly in practice but treated as simple interest on each monthly deposit for the purpose of the syllabus. The relationship between the sub‑concepts is: each monthly deposit earns interest for a different number of months — the first deposit earns interest for n months, the second for n‑1 months, …, the last deposit earns interest for 1 month. Summing these individual interests yields the total interest I = P × n(n+1)/2 × (r/12)/100. Adding the principal sum P×n gives the maturity value M = P×n + I. This formula links the recurring deposit account (node) to the interest computation (node) and is the core quantitative tool for RD problems in the ICSE examination.
steps: The maturity value of a recurring deposit equals the total principal deposited plus the simple interest earned on each instalment for the months it stays in the account.
Here is why: each monthly deposit earns interest for a different duration — the first deposit works for the whole term, the last deposit works for only one month.
The sum of the first n natural numbers, n(n+1)/2, captures this decreasing pattern.
Multiplying by the monthly interest rate (r/12)/100 converts the sum of months into rupees of interest.
Adding the principal P×n gives the final amount.

cards.title: Interest computation for a Recurring Deposit (RD) determines the total interest…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Interest computation for a Recurring Deposit (RD) determines the total interest earned on a series of equal monthly instalments deposited over a fixed tenure at a given annual rate. Let the monthly instalment be P (₹), the number of months be n, and the annual interest rate be r % per annum. Each instalment earns simple interest for the remaining months: the first instalment earns interest for n months, the second for n-1 months, …, the last for 1 month. Summing this arithmetic series yields the total interest I = P × (n(n+1))/(2) × (r)/(12 × 100). The maturity value M is the sum of all instalments plus interest: M = nP + I. This formula links the three sub‑concepts — recurring deposit accounts (regular monthly deposits), maturity value formula (total amount received), and interest computation (the focus of this node) — by showing how the periodic deposits and the time‑weighted interest combine to produce the final payout.

Monthly deposit P = 500 ₹, tenure n = 12 months, annual rate r = 8 %.
Stage 2 – Understand the time each instalment stays.
The first ₹500 stays for 12 months, the second for 11 months, …, the twelfth for 1 month.
If we wrote simple interest for each, we would have 12 separate calculations.

cards.title: A Recurring Deposit (RD) account is a banking product where a fixed sum…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Recurring Deposit (RD) account is a banking product where a fixed sum (monthly installment, denoted P) is deposited every month for a predetermined period (n months) at a fixed annual interest rate (r%). The maturity value (M) is the sum of all installments plus the interest earned on each installment for the months it remains in the account. The standard formula for maturity value is M = P × n + P × n(n+1)/2 × r/(12×100). This node focuses on algebraic manipulation of that formula to solve for any one unknown variable — P, r, or n — when the other three are known. The relationship is linear in P and r, but quadratic in n because the term n(n+1) appears. Solving for n requires solving a quadratic equation and selecting the positive integer root that makes sense in the context of months. The concept builds directly on the maturity value formula and interest computation covered in earlier nodes, extending them to inverse problems typical of ICSE board questions.
steps: The RD maturity formula can be rearranged to find any unknown variable — monthly deposit, rate, or time — by treating it as a linear or quadratic equation in that unknown.

Here is why: The formula M = P[n + n(n+1)r/2400] contains three variables (P, r, n) besides the known maturity value M. When P is unknown, the equation is linear in P because P appears only as a factor.
When r is unknown, it is also linear because r appears only in the term multiplied by P. When n is unknown, the term n(n+1) makes it quadratic.

Recognising the algebraic nature of each case tells you which solving technique to use. Consider a typical ICSE problem: "A person deposits ₹x per month for 2 years at 8% p.a. and gets ₹50,000 at maturity.
The linear structure makes this straightforward.

cards.title: In a recurring deposit (RD) account…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a recurring deposit (RD) account, a fixed sum of money (the monthly installment P) is deposited at the end of each month for a period of n months. The bank pays interest at an annual rate r (percent per annum) on each installment for the time it remains in the account. The maturity value M is the total amount receivable at the end of the n‑th month, comprising the sum of all principal deposits and the interest earned on them. The interest on each installment is calculated as simple interest for the number of months it stays deposited. The first installment earns interest for n months, the second for n‑1 months, …, the last installment for 1 month. The sum of this arithmetic progression is n(n+1)/2 months‑equivalent. Converting the annual rate to a monthly decimal gives r/(12×100)=r/1200. Hence the total interest I = P × [n(n+1)/2] × (r/1200). The maturity value is therefore M = Pn + P\;(n(n+1))/(2)\;(r)/(1200). All quantities are in SI‑compatible units: P in rupees (₹), n is dimensionless (count of months), r in percent (% per annum), and M in rupees (₹). This formula links the four variables; knowing any three allows determination of the fourth.

Here is why: 1.
The formula is linear in P, so isolating P requires only division by a known factor. 2.
The formula is linear in r, allowing direct isolation of r by simple division. 3.
The formula is quadratic in n (because the interest term contains n²), which leads to a quadratic equation solvable by the quadratic formula or factoring. 4.
Real‑world RD problems frequently give the maturity value and ask for the missing deposit amount, period, or rate, making this skill essential for exams and daily financial planning. 5.

cards.title: A premature withdrawal (or premature closure) of a Recurring Deposit (RD)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A premature withdrawal (or premature closure) of a Recurring Deposit (RD) account occurs when the depositor closes the account before the agreed maturity period. In the CISCE ICSE Class 10 Commercial Mathematics curriculum, the standard RD uses simple interest calculated monthly at a fixed annual rate r% for the full term n months. If the account is closed after k months (k < n), the bank typically pays interest at the prevailing savings bank rate r_s% (which is lower than r%) for the actual period the money was held. Additionally, most banks levy a penalty — often a percentage of the interest earned or a flat charge — which is deducted before the final payout. The revised maturity value (MV_pre) is therefore: MV_pre = Total Principal Deposited + Interest at Savings Rate – Penalty where Total Principal Deposited = P × k (monthly installment P times number of months k), Interest at Savings Rate = P × k(k+1)/2 × (r_s/12)/100 (simple interest on each monthly deposit for the remaining months up to k), Penalty = as per bank rules (e.g., 1% of interest earned, or a fixed ₹50–₹100). This concept extends the basic RD maturity value formula (covered in nodes and) to real‑world situations where liquidity needs force early closure. It connects the interest computation technique (monthly simple interest on a series of deposits) with the practical adjustment of rate and penalty.
steps: Premature withdrawal reduces the maturity value because the bank pays interest at a lower savings rate and usually deducts a penalty.
Here is why: the bank plans its lending based on the committed term; early closure disrupts that plan, so it discourages it by offering a less attractive rate and a penalty.

After 12 months you need the money.
The bank will not give you the 8% interest for those 12 months; instead it pays the savings account rate, say 4% p.a., and may charge a penalty of 1% on the interest earned.

cards.title: A Recurring Deposit (RD) account is a time‑deposit scheme where a fixed amount…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Recurring Deposit (RD) account is a time‑deposit scheme where a fixed amount P (monthly instalment) is deposited at the end of each month for n months at an annual interest rate r percent. The bank computes interest on each instalment for the remaining months using simple interest, because each instalment stays for a different duration. The total interest I is the sum of simple interests on all instalments: I = P × n(n+1)/2 × (r/12)/100. The maturity value M is the sum of all deposits plus interest: M = P × n + I. Key relationships: the formula assumes monthly compounding is not used; interest is calculated on a monthly basis but credited at maturity. The variables are: P (monthly deposit in ₹), n (number of months), r (annual rate in %). The chapter also covers variations such as quarterly deposits or mid‑term withdrawals, but the core ICSE syllabus focuses on the standard monthly RD with simple interest.
steps: The one thing to remember: every ICSE RD problem reduces to the single formula M = Pn + P·n(n+1)/2 × r/(1200); master its algebraic rearrangements and you solve any variant.
Here is why: (1) The formula encapsulates the entire chapter — deposits, time, rate, and interest.
(2) ICSE exams test three question types: direct maturity value, finding missing variable (P, n, or r), and comparing two RD offers.
(3) All three types are solved by substituting knowns into the same formula and rearranging.
(4) The only arithmetic trap is the factor 1200 (12 months × 100 for percent).
(5) Word problems often hide the monthly rate or give annual rate; always convert.

cards.title: Shares and Dividends is a commercial mathematics chapter that introduces the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Shares and Dividends is a commercial mathematics chapter that introduces the financial terminology and calculations used when individuals invest in company shares. The core quantities are: Face Value (FV) – the nominal value printed on the share certificate; Market Value (MV) – the price at which the share is bought or sold in the stock market; Premium – the amount by which MV exceeds FV; Discount – the amount by which MV is less than FV. Dividend is the portion of profit distributed per share, usually expressed as a percentage of FV. Income from shares equals dividend per share multiplied by the number of shares held. Yield (or Return) measures the effectiveness of the investment: (Annual Dividend Income ÷ Total Investment) × 100 %. The chapter links these concepts: FV and MV determine premium/discount; dividend percentage applies to FV; income depends on number of shares; yield compares income to the actual money invested (MV × number of shares). Mastery requires fluency in moving between these quantities, applying percentage formulas, and interpreting results in real‑world investment decisions.
steps: The yield of an investment is the most accurate measure of performance because it compares the actual annual income earned against the total capital invested.
Understanding this chapter requires mastering six key concepts: Face Value, Market Value, Premium, Discount, Dividend, and Yield.
These terms function as the language of the stock market, allowing investors to translate company announcements into personal financial outcomes.
Face Value represents the nominal cost printed on a share, while Market Value is the actual price paid on the exchange, which fluctuates based on company performance.
Dividends are calculated strictly as a percentage of the Face Value, meaning the dividend amount per share remains constant regardless of the market price.
The Yield formula accounts for the premium or discount paid, revealing whether the investment is efficient compared to the declared dividend rate.

cards.title: Face value (FV), also called nominal value or par value…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Face value (FV), also called nominal value or par value, is the fixed monetary amount printed on a share certificate by the issuing company. It is denoted by the symbol FV and measured in Indian rupees (₹). The face value remains constant throughout the life of the share unless the company undergoes a stock split or consolidation, which are corporate actions covered in higher classes. Key relationships: - Dividend calculation: The dividend declared by a company is always expressed as a percentage of the face value. For a dividend rate r % the dividend per share = (r × FV)/100. - Market value (MV): The price at which the share trades in the stock market; it can be above (premium), equal to (par), or below (discount) the face value. - Premium/Discount: When MV > FV the share is at a premium; when MV < FV it is at a discount. These concepts are treated in sibling nodes and. - Income and yield: The actual return an investor earns depends on the purchase price (MV) and the dividend based on FV; yield = (Dividend per share ÷ MV) × 100. This is covered in node. Face value is therefore the anchor for all dividend‑related arithmetic in commercial mathematics.
steps: Let’s walk through the idea of face value step by step, linking it to what you already know from the chapter overview. 1.
What a share looks like – When a company issues shares, each certificate (or electronic entry) carries a printed number, e.g.
“Face Value ₹10”.
Think of it like the MRP printed on a packet of biscuits: the manufacturer says “this packet is worth ₹10”.
The company uses this number for all its internal accounting. 2.
Why it matters for dividends – Suppose the board declares a 12 % dividend.
cards.misconception: This misconception often arises from confusing a split with a bonus issue, where additional shares are given free, increasing total face value.

cards.title: Market value (MV) of a share is the current price at which the share is bought…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Market value (MV) of a share is the current price at which the share is bought or sold in the stock market. It is a dynamic quantity determined by demand and supply, company performance, investor sentiment, and macro‑economic factors. In the ICSE Commercial Mathematics framework, market value is related to the face value (FV) (also called nominal or par value) by the simple linear relations: - If the share trades above face value, it is at a premium: MV = FV + Premium. - If the share trades below face value, it is at a discount: MV = FV – Discount. Market value is always expressed in the same monetary unit as face value (Indian rupees, ₹). Unlike face value, which is fixed at issuance, market value fluctuates continuously during trading hours. The concept of market value is foundational for computing the investment cost, dividend yield, and capital gain/loss in later nodes. It does not include brokerage, taxes, or transaction charges — those are treated separately in practical problems.
steps: Market value is the actual price at which a share is traded on the stock exchange, while face value is the fixed, unchanging price printed on the share certificate.
Market value fluctuates based on investor demand and company performance, whereas face value remains constant.

A premium occurs when the market value exceeds the face value, representing the extra amount buyers are willing to pay. A discount occurs when the market value is less than the face value, representing the shortfall…

Market value is the essential figure for calculating the actual cost of an investment, as it reflects the current price in the market.

cards.title: Premium and discount describe the relationship between a share’s market value…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Premium and discount describe the relationship between a share’s market value (MV) and its face value (FV). - Premium occurs when MV > FV. The premium amount = MV – FV. Premium percent = (Premium / FV) × 100. - Discount occurs when MV < FV. The discount amount = FV – MV. Discount percent = (Discount / FV) × 100. - When MV = FV, the share is said to be at par (neither premium nor discount). These concepts link directly to the earlier nodes: face value is the nominal value printed on the share certificate; market value is the price at which the share trades in the market. Premium/discount quantifies the deviation of market value from face value and is essential for computing the actual investment cost, dividend yield, and capital gain/loss in later nodes (dividend calculation, income and yield).
steps: Premium and discount are determined by comparing the market value (MV) of a share to its fixed face value (FV).

The core principle is that all percentage deviations are calculated relative to the face value, not the market price. - Premium represents an investment cost above the nominal value, indicating high market demand.
Discount represents an investment cost below the nominal value, often reflecting market caution.
The face value remains the constant base for all percentage calculations, ensuring consistency in financial reporting.

cards.title: Dividend calculation in the context of shares refers to determining the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Dividend calculation in the context of shares refers to determining the monetary return a shareholder receives from a company's declared dividend. The dividend is always expressed as a percentage of the face value (also called nominal value) of a share, not its market value. If a company declares a dividend of D% and the face value of each share is FV, then the dividend per share (DPS) is given by DPS = (D/100) × FV. For an investor holding N shares, the total dividend income (TD) equals DPS × N = (D × FV × N)/100. This calculation is independent of whether the shares were bought at a premium, at par, or at a discount; the market price influences the investor's yield but not the dividend amount itself. The concept links directly to the earlier nodes: face value provides the base amount, market value and premium/discount explain purchase price variations, while dividend calculation uses only the face value and the declared rate. Understanding this distinction is crucial for later computation of yield and comparison of investment options.
steps: Dividends are always calculated as a strict percentage of a share's face value, completely independent of the market price paid by the investor.
First, dividends represent a corporate payout tied strictly to nominal capital rather than market valuation.
Second, isolating the face value prevents common student calculation errors regarding premium or discount prices.
Third, a standardized two-step formula ensures reliable computation regardless of fluctuating stock prices.
Fourth, mastering this foundational corporate action directly prepares students for advanced yield and return calculations.

cards.title: Income from shares is the total dividend received by a shareholder in a given…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Income from shares is the total dividend received by a shareholder in a given period, usually one year. It is calculated as the product of the number of shares held, the face value (nominal value) of each share, and the dividend rate declared by the company, divided by 100. Mathematically, Annual Income = (Number of shares × Face Value × Dividend%) / 100. Yield, also called return on investment, expresses this income as a percentage of the actual capital invested. The capital invested equals the number of shares multiplied by the market value (the price at which the share is bought or sold). Therefore, Yield% = (Annual Income / (Number of shares × Market Value)) × 100. Substituting the income formula gives Yield% = (Dividend% × Face Value) / Market Value × 100. This shows that yield depends on the dividend rate, the face value, and the market price; a higher market price reduces yield for the same dividend. The concepts of face value, market value, premium/discount, and dividend calculation (covered in earlier nodes) are all linked here: face value determines the dividend amount, market value determines the investment cost, and premium or discount indicates whether the market value is above or below face value. Understanding income and yield allows an investor to compare different shares and decide which offers a better return on the money actually spent.
steps: Let’s walk through the idea of income and yield from shares step by step, linking what you already know.
First, recall the face value (also called nominal value) — the original value printed on the share certificate, e.g., ₹10.
The market value is the price you actually pay in the stock market; it can be higher (premium) or lower (discount) than the face value.
The company declares a dividend as a percentage of the face value, say 15%.
That means for every share of face value ₹10, the company pays ₹1.50 per year (15% of ₹10).
If you own N shares, your annual dividend income is simply N × (Dividend% × Face Value / 100).

cards.title: In the context of shares and dividends, the key quantities are face value (FV)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In the context of shares and dividends, the key quantities are face value (FV), market value (MV), dividend rate (r), number of shares (n), dividend per share (D), total income (I), investment (Inv), and yield percentage (Y). Face value is the nominal value printed on the share certificate, used to compute dividend. Market value is the actual price at which the share is bought or sold in the stock market; it may be at par, at a premium (MV > FV) or at a discount (MV < FV). Dividend rate is the percentage of face value declared by the company as profit distribution. Dividend per share = (FV × r)/100. Total income from holding n shares is I = n × D = (FV × r × n)/100. Investment required to buy n shares is Inv = n × MV. Yield percentage measures the return on investment and is given by Y = (I/Inv) × 100 = [(FV × r × n)/100] ÷ (n × MV) × 100 = (FV × r)/MV. Thus yield depends only on face value, dividend rate, and market value, independent of the number of shares. These relationships allow one to solve for any unknown when the others are known, forming the basis of multi‑step problems in this chapter.

cards.title: A linear inequation in one variable is an algebraic statement of the form ax +…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A linear inequation in one variable is an algebraic statement of the form ax + b \; \; c where a, b, c ∈ R, a ≠ 0, x is the unknown, and represents any of the four inequality symbols <, ≤, >, ≥. The solution set consists of all real numbers that make the statement true. Two standard ways to describe this set are set‑builder notation {x ∈ R condition} and interval notation (e.g., (-∞, 5]). The number‑line representation shades the portion of the real line that satisfies the inequation, using an open circle for strict inequalities and a closed circle for inclusive ones. This chapter also covers the properties of inequalities (addition, subtraction, multiplication/division by positive or negative numbers) and applies them to solve word problems involving budgets, distances, and age constraints.

cards.title: A linear inequation in one variable is an algebraic statement that relates a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A linear inequation in one variable is an algebraic statement that relates a linear expression in a single unknown to a constant using one of the inequality symbols `<`, `>`, `≤`, or `≥`. Formally, it can be written as `ax + b < c`, `ax + b > c`, `ax + b ≤ c`, or `ax + b ≥ c`, where `a`, `b`, `c` are real numbers and `a ≠ 0`. The variable `x` represents the unknown quantity. The solution set consists of all real values of `x` that make the inequality true. Key relationships: - Adding or subtracting the same real number to both sides preserves the inequality direction. - Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive real number preserves the direction; multiplying or dividing by a negative real number reverses the direction. - The solution can be expressed in set notation (e.g., `{ x ∈ ℝ | x < 5 }`) or graphically on a number line (open/closed circles and arrows). This node focuses only on forming, simplifying, and solving such inequations; representation in set notation and on the number line is covered in the next node.
steps: The one thing to remember: Solving a linear inequation is exactly like solving a linear equation, except you must flip the inequality sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number.
Here is why: the order of numbers on the real line reverses when multiplied by a negative; e.g., `3 < 5` but `-3 > -5`.

The total marks will be `12 + x`.
The condition “at least 35” translates to `12 + x ≥ 35`.

cards.title: A linear inequation in one variable
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A linear inequation in one variable (e.g., ax + b < c) has a solution set consisting of all real numbers that satisfy the inequality. This solution set can be expressed in three equivalent forms. Set‑builder notation writes the set as {x ∈ R condition on x}, explicitly stating the variable, the universal set (usually R), and the inequality condition. Interval notation uses brackets and parentheses to denote the same set compactly: a square bracket [ or ) means the endpoint is included (corresponding to ≤ or ≥), while a round bracket ( or ) means the endpoint is excluded (corresponding to < or >). For unbounded intervals, ∞ or -∞ always takes a round bracket. Number line representation draws a horizontal line representing R; a solid dot (●) marks an included endpoint, a hollow dot (○) marks an excluded endpoint, and a thick line or arrow shades all numbers that satisfy the inequation. When two inequations are combined with “and” (intersection), the solution is the overlap of their individual representations; with “or” (union), it is the combined shaded regions. Mastery of these three forms allows seamless translation between algebraic, symbolic, and graphical descriptions of the same solution set.
steps: The solution to a linear inequation is a range of real numbers, and you must be able to express this range using three standard ICSE formats: set-builder notation, interval notation, and the number line.

The vertical bar represents the phrase "such that," defining the condition for all real numbers x. Interval notation provides a compact way to describe the range.
Because x < 4 includes all numbers up to 4 but excludes 4 itself, you write (-∞, 4).
The round bracket at 4 indicates exclusion.
If the condition were x ≤ 4, you would use a square bracket: (-∞, 4].
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., [-2, ∞)) reveals the misconception that the brackets can be chosen freely, when each bracket must mirror exactly whether the endpoint satisfies the inequality.

The general form is ax + b < c, ax + b > c, ax + b ≤ c, or ax + b ≥ c, where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0. The solution set consists of all real values of x that make the inequation true. The solution can be expressed in set-builder notation {x ∈ ℝ | condition} or interval notation, and represented on a number line using open circles for strict inequalities (<, >) and closed circles for inclusive inequalities (≤, ≥). cards.definition: A compound linear inequation in one variable consists of two simple linear inequations connected by the logical words “and” (conjunction) or “or” (disjunction). - For “and”, the solution set is the intersection of the individual solution sets: a number must satisfy both inequations simultaneously. Each simple inequation is solved algebraically (remembering to reverse the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative number). The resulting intervals are then combined using intersection or union. The final answer is expressed in set notation (e.g., { x ∈ ℝ | 2 < x ≤ 5 }) and represented on a number line with open circles for strict inequalities ( <, > ) and closed circles for inclusive inequalities ( ≤, ≥ ). cards.title: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c =…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0. The chapter builds on this definition by introducing three interconnected ideas. First, the nature of roots is governed by the discriminant Δ = b^2 - 4ac; if Δ > 0 the equation has two distinct real roots, if Δ = 0 it has two equal real roots, and if Δ < 0 the roots are non‑real complex conjugates. Second, solving methods include factorisation (splitting the middle term), completing the square, and the quadratic formula x = (-b ± √(Δ))/(2a); each method is a different algebraic pathway to the same roots. Third, word problems translate everyday situations — such as projectile motion, area‑perimeter puzzles, or profit‑loss scenarios — into quadratic equations, requiring the student to formulate the equation, choose an appropriate solving technique, and interpret the roots in context. Together these sub‑concepts form a complete toolkit: the discriminant tells what to expect, the solving techniques tell how to obtain the roots, and the word‑problem framework tells why the roots matter in practical terms.
steps: The quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 is the mathematical foundation for describing parabolic paths, such as the arc of a kite in flight.
The coefficient a dictates the parabola's direction, while the discriminant Δ = b^2 - 4ac serves as a predictive tool for the roots.
Three distinct algebraic methods—factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula—offer varying levels of efficiency for finding roots.
Word problems bridge the gap between abstract algebra and physical reality, requiring the translation of geometric or motion-based constraints into solvable equations.
Mastery of these concepts is essential for ICSE examinations, which test the ability to formulate, solve, and interpret quadratic models.

cards.title: A quadratic equation in standard form is ax^2 + bx + c = 0 where a, b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A quadratic equation in standard form is ax^2 + bx + c = 0 where a, b, c ∈ R and a ≠ 0. The discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac determines the nature of its roots without solving the equation. - If D > 0, the equation has two distinct real roots given by (-b ± √(D))/(2a). - If D = 0, the equation has two equal real roots (a repeated root) -(b)/(2a). - If D < 0, the equation has two complex conjugate roots (-b ± i√(|D|))/(2a) with non‑zero imaginary parts. The discriminant also reveals the graph of y = ax^2 + bx + c: D > 0 means the parabola cuts the x‑axis at two points; D = 0 means it touches the x‑axis at the vertex; D < 0 means it lies entirely above (if a>0) or below (if a<0) the x‑axis. The sign of a decides the opening direction, while D decides intersection with the axis. This concept links the algebraic expression to its geometric representation and is foundational for solving quadratics by formula, factorisation, and for tackling word problems where the nature of roots dictates feasibility (e.g., time cannot be negative or imaginary).
steps: The discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac is the single number that tells you everything about the roots of a quadratic equation without actually finding them.
Here is why: the quadratic formula (-b ± √(b^2-4ac))/(2a) shows that the square‑root term √(D) decides whether the roots are real and distinct (D>0), real and equal (D=0), or non‑real (D<0).
The sign of a only flips the parabola;
D decides its x‑axis intersections.
Consider the equation 2x^2 - 4x + 2 = 0.

cards.title: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0 where a,b,c∈ R and a≠0. Solving it means finding all real values of x that satisfy the equality. Two standard algebraic techniques are taught in this node: 1. Factorisation – rewriting the quadratic as a product of two linear factors (px+q)(rx+s)=0 by splitting the middle term or by inspection, then applying the zero‑product property px+q=0 or rx+s=0. This method works efficiently when the discriminant D=b^2-4ac is a perfect square and the coefficients are small integers. 2. Quadratic formula – a universal derivation from completing the square: x=(-b±√(b^2-4ac))/(2a) The expression under the square root, D=b^2-4ac, is the discriminant. Its sign determines the nature of roots (already covered in the previous node): D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 gives one real repeated root, D<0 gives no real roots (complex roots are not required for ICSE Class 10). Both methods are algebraically equivalent; factorisation is a shortcut when the quadratic is “nice”, while the formula guarantees a solution for any real coefficients. The node also emphasises checking solutions by substitution and presenting answers in the required form (simplified fractions or decimals as per the question).

Step 3: Split the middle term – Rewrite 7x as 6x+x: 2x^2+6x+x+3=0.

cards.title: A word problem in quadratic equations requires translating a verbal description…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A word problem in quadratic equations requires translating a verbal description into a mathematical model where the unknown quantity satisfies a quadratic equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0 (a≠0). The process involves: (1) identifying the unknown and assigning a variable (usually x); (2) expressing all other quantities in terms of that variable using the given relationships (area = length × breadth, distance = speed × time, work = rate × time, etc.); (3) forming an equation that reflects the condition (equality, sum, difference, product); (4) simplifying to the standard quadratic form; (5) solving the quadratic by factorisation or the quadratic formula x=(-b±√(b^2-4ac))/(2a); (6) interpreting the roots in the context — discarding negative, zero, or extraneous values that do not make physical sense (e.g., negative length, time, or speed). The discriminant D=b^2-4ac from the nature‑of‑roots node tells whether the problem yields two distinct real solutions, one repeated solution, or no real solution, which directly affects the feasibility of the real‑world scenario. This node builds on the solving techniques of node and the discriminant analysis of node, applying them to contextual situations such as geometry (area/perimeter), motion (speed‑time‑distance), numbers (sum/product/reciprocal), work‑rate, and age problems.
steps: Let’s walk through a typical ICSE word problem step by step.
Step 1 – Read and visualise.
Picture the situation: “A train travels 360 km at a uniform speed.
If the speed had been 5 km/h more, it would have taken 1 hour less.
Find the original speed.” Draw a mental timeline: two journeys, same distance, different speeds and times.
Step 2 – Choose the variable.

cards.title: A parameterised quadratic equation is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A parameterised quadratic equation is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 where at least one coefficient (a, b, or c) contains an unknown constant, usually denoted by k, m, or p. The discriminant D = b² – 4ac remains the key quantity that determines the nature of the roots. For a parameterised equation, D becomes an algebraic expression in the parameter. The conditions are: - Real and distinct roots ⇔ D > 0 - Real and equal roots ⇔ D = 0 - No real roots (complex conjugate pair) ⇔ D < 0 Because the coefficient of x² must be non‑zero for the equation to be quadratic, any parameter value that makes a = 0 must be excluded even if it satisfies the discriminant condition. The relationship between the coefficients and the roots (sum = –b/a, product = c/a) also holds and can be used to form equations with given root properties. This node builds directly on the nature of roots (node 002) and the solving methods (node 003) by treating the discriminant as a function of the parameter and solving the resulting inequality or equation for the parameter.
steps: The discriminant D = b² – 4ac dictates the nature of roots for any quadratic equation, even when coefficients are defined by a parameter k. - The discriminant acts as a diagnostic tool: D < 0 results in no real roots, D…
The parameter k functions as a variable that adjusts the discriminant, allowing you to solve for specific root conditions by setting up equations or inequalities.
The quadratic requirement is absolute: even if a value of k satisfies the discriminant condition, it must be discarded if it results in a = 0, as the equation would cease to be quadratic.
Systematic verification is required: always check the leading coefficient against the zero-value constraint to ensure the integrity of the quadratic form.

cards.title: Equations reducible to quadratic form are algebraic equations that are not…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Equations reducible to quadratic form are algebraic equations that are not quadratic in the given variable but can be converted into a standard quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) through an appropriate substitution. The substitution replaces a composite expression (such as x + 1/x, x^2 + 1/x^2, √x, or an exponential term like 2^x) with a new variable, say y. The original equation then becomes a quadratic in y, which can be solved by factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula. After obtaining the values of y, back-substitution yields the values of the original variable, often requiring the solution of additional simple equations. This concept extends the applicability of quadratic techniques to a wider class of problems, including reciprocal equations, equations involving radicals, and certain exponential equations. It relies on the discriminant and nature of roots concepts from the quadratic chapter, and it connects to the word problems node where real-life situations lead to such reducible equations. The key steps are: identify a suitable substitution, rewrite the equation as a quadratic in the new variable, solve for the new variable, and then solve for the original variable, checking for extraneous roots introduced by the substitution.
steps: The core takeaway is that you can solve complex equations by identifying a repeating "chunk," substituting it with a new variable to form a simple quadratic, and then back-substituting to find the original values.
Substitution transforms high-degree or complex algebraic structures into manageable quadratic forms.
Recognizing patterns like reciprocal pairs (x + 1/x) or identical polynomial blocks is the primary skill required.
Back-substitution is mandatory to translate the solution of the new variable back into the original variable.
Verification is essential because the substitution process can introduce extraneous roots that do not satisfy the original equation.
To solve an equation like x^2 + 1/x^2 - 3(x + 1/x) + 2 = 0, first identify the repeating pattern.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., y = x^2 + 1/x^2) reveals the misconception that the substitution must directly replace the highest-degree term, ignoring the algebraic relationship between the expressions.
remember: Identify the substitution that reduces the equation (x^2 + 1/x^2) - 5(x + 1/x) + 6 = 0 to a quadratic equation.
Explain why the equation √(x+3) + √(x-2) = 5 can be solved by reducing to a quadratic, and outline the substitution steps without solving completely.
Evaluate the claim: "Every equation containing a term like x + 1/x can be reduced to a quadratic by substituting y = x + 1/x." Provide a counterexample if false.

cards.title: A quadratic equation in standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0).
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A quadratic equation in standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). Its roots α and β satisfy Vieta’s formulas: α + β = –b/a and αβ = c/a. Given any two numbers α and β (real, irrational, or complex), the monic quadratic equation having them as roots is x² – (α+β)x + αβ = 0; any non‑zero constant multiple of this equation also has the same roots. This node focuses on constructing quadratic equations from given roots and on evaluating symmetric functions of roots — such as α²+β², α³+β³, 1/α+1/β — using only the sum and product, without explicitly solving for α and β. It also covers forming new equations whose roots are transformations of the original roots (e.g., α+k, kα, α², 1/α). These techniques rely on algebraic identities: α²+β² = (α+β)² – 2αβ, α³+β³ = (α+β)³ – 3αβ(α+β), and 1/α+1/β = (α+β)/(αβ). The concept connects the solving methods of Node 003 and the reducible equations of Node 006 to advanced problem‑solving and synthesis in Node 008.
steps: The core takeaway is that any quadratic equation is uniquely defined by the sum and product of its roots, allowing you to construct equations or evaluate symmetric expressions without solving for the roots themselves.
Supporting arguments:
Vieta’s formulas provide a direct bridge between the coefficients of an equation and the sum and product of its roots.
Algebraic identities allow for the conversion of complex symmetric functions into simple expressions of the sum and product.
Root transformation techniques enable the derivation of new equations from existing ones by applying algebraic shifts to the sum and product.
This approach is computationally efficient, avoiding the need to handle potentially messy irrational or complex roots directly.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., x² – x – 6 = 0) reveals the misconception that the sum is copied with its own sign into the middle term — the formula already subtracts the sum, so –(–1) must become +1.
remember: Write the quadratic equation whose roots are 2 and –3.
If α and β are the roots of 2x² – 5x + 3 = 0, find the value of α² + β² without solving the equation.
A student claims that if the roots of x² – 4x + 4 = 0 are α and β, then the equation with roots α+1 and β+1 is x² – 6x + 9 = 0. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A quadratic equation in one variable is an equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0 where a,b,c∈ R and a≠0. Its nature of roots is decided by the discriminant D=b^2-4ac: D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 gives two equal real roots, D<0 gives no real roots (complex conjugate pair). The quadratic formula x=(-b±√(D))/(2a) provides the exact roots for any a,b,c. Factorisation rewrites the quadratic as (px+q)(rx+s)=0 when the middle term can be split into two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b. Word problems translate real‑life situations (area, speed‑time, profit‑loss, age) into a quadratic equation, solve it, and interpret the roots in context. This synthesis node connects the three solution strategies, highlights the decision tree (check discriminant → choose factorisation if easy → otherwise use formula), and maps the typical ICSE question patterns: direct solve, nature‑of‑roots justification, formation from word statement, and application in geometry or motion problems.
steps: Efficiency in the exam hall depends on choosing the right method for the specific quadratic equation provided. - The discriminant acts as a diagnostic tool to determine the nature of roots before solving.
Factorisation is the fastest method when the discriminant is a perfect square.
The quadratic formula is the universal fallback for complex or non-factorable equations.
Contextual constraints in word problems often require rejecting mathematically valid but physically impossible roots.
ICSE examiners prioritize clear, stepwise logical progression over raw calculation.
To solve 2x^2-7x+3=0, first identify a=2, b=-7, c=3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., x^2-3x-28=0) reveals the misconception that the sum is copied with its own sign into the middle term — the formula x^2 - Sx + P already negates the sum, so a negative sum must appear as a positive coefficient.
remember: State the quadratic formula and the discriminant for the equation ax^2+bx+c=0.
Given the equation 5x^2-3x+1=0, determine the nature of its roots without solving.

cards.title: A proportion is an equality of two ratios.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A proportion is an equality of two ratios. If four quantities a, b, c, d (all non‑zero and of the same kind) satisfy (a)/(b) = (c)/(d) we write a:b = c:d or a:b::c:d and say “a, b, c, d are in proportion”. The first and fourth terms (a and d) are called extremes; the second and third (b and c) are means. The fundamental property is product of extremes = product of means: a × d = b × c. Proportion is the gateway to continued proportion (three quantities where the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third), mean proportional (the middle term of a continued proportion), and the algebraic properties componendo, dividendo, alternendo, invertendo which are derived by manipulating the basic equality (a)/(b)=(c)/(d). Direct applications include solving problems on similar figures, mixtures, speed‑time‑distance, and scaling in maps or models.
steps: The one thing to remember: A proportion is simply two equal ratios, and its most useful test is “product of extremes = product of means”.
Here is why: a ratio compares two quantities of the same kind; a proportion states that two such comparisons give the same relative size.
Because (a)/(b)=(c)/(d) is equivalent to ad=bc, we can check proportionality without dividing — just cross‑multiply.
Consider a map where 1 cm represents 5 km. If two cities are 3 cm apart on the map, the real distance x satisfies 1:5 = 3:x.
Cross‑multiplying gives 1 × x = 5 × 3 → x = 15 km. The same step works for any scaling problem: recipe ingredients, similar triangles, or currency conversion.
Now imagine a student sees 2:3 = 4:6.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “No, because 8/12 ≠ 18/27”) reveals the misconception that one must simplify each ratio separately instead of using the cross‑product test, which is faster and less error‑prone.
remember: State whether the numbers 8, 12, 18, 27 are in proportion.
If x, 15, 20, 25 are in proportion, find x.
A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How many cups of sugar are needed if 9 cups of flour are used.

cards.title: Three non‑zero quantities a, b, c are said to be in continued proportion when…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Three non‑zero quantities a, b, c are said to be in continued proportion when the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third, i.e. (a)/(b) = (b)/(c). Cross‑multiplying gives the defining relation b^2=ac. The middle term b is called the mean proportional between a and c (treated in the next node). Continued proportion extends naturally to longer chains a:b = b:c = c:d =; each adjacent pair satisfies the same square‑product rule. The concept links directly to the basic proportion a:b = c:d studied earlier: a continued proportion is a special case where the two ratios share a common term. In algebraic work, the equation b^2=ac is the primary tool for finding an unknown term when the other two are known, and for verifying whether three given numbers form a continued proportion.
steps: A continued proportion exists when three numbers have their first-to-second ratio equal to their second-to-third ratio, governed by the central symmetry of the square-product rule b^2=ac.
The symmetry of the middle term appearing twice as denominator and numerator causes its square to equal the product of the extremes.
The two ratios can be represented visually as equal arcs in a row of three terms.
Missing terms in any algebraic set of lengths, speeds, or currency can be solved using the square-product equation.
Real-world quantities like Indian kitchen recipes for rice, water, and broth verify continued proportions by matching b^2 with ac.
A ladder analogy illustrates that the relative distance from the first rung to the second equals the distance from the second to the third.
remember: State the condition that three numbers x, y, z must satisfy to be in continued proportion.
Are the numbers 5, 10, 20 in continued proportion? Justify your answer.
If a, 12, 27 are in continued proportion, find the value of a.

cards.title: In a continued proportion three quantities a, b, c satisfy a:b = b:c.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a continued proportion three quantities a, b, c satisfy a:b = b:c. The middle term b is called the mean proportional (or geometric mean) between a and c. Algebraically, b^2 = a × c so b = √(ac). The mean proportional exists only when a and c have the same sign (both positive or both negative) because a real square‑root is required. It is a special case of the geometric mean for two numbers and links directly to the concept of continued proportion (node). If a, b, c are in continued proportion, then b is the mean proportional; conversely, if b = √(ac) then a, b, c are in continued proportion. The mean proportional is dimensionally consistent: if a and c carry units (e.g., metres, kilograms), b carries the same unit.
steps: The mean proportional is the geometric middle term that keeps the ratio between three numbers perfectly constant. - It is derived from the continued proportion a:b = b:c, which simplifies to b^2 = ac.
It acts as a geometric bridge, ensuring the ratio of the first to the second equals the ratio of the second to the third.
It is dimensionally consistent, meaning the result carries the same units as the input values.
It is distinct from the arithmetic mean, as it relies on multiplication and square roots rather than addition and division.
To find the mean proportional, first identify the two extreme values (a and c).
Multiply these two numbers together to get their product.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., x = 13, the arithmetic mean of 8 and 18) reveals the misconception that ‘continued proportion’ behaves like an arithmetic progression, when the middle term must satisfy a multiplicative relation, x^2 = ac, not x = (a+c)/2.
remember: What is the mean proportional between 5 and 20.
If 8, x, 18 are in continued proportion, find x.
Evaluate the statement: “The mean proportional between two numbers is always smaller than the larger number.”.

cards.title: Componendo is a property of proportions stating that if four quantities a, b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Componendo is a property of proportions stating that if four quantities a, b, c, d are in proportion (a/b = c/d), then the sum of the first and second terms divided by the second term equals the sum of the third and fourth terms divided by the fourth term: (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d. It follows directly from the definition of proportion and cross‑multiplication. In a continued proportion a:b = b:c, componendo gives (a+b)/b = (b+c)/c, linking it to mean proportional concepts. The property is symmetric: applying componendo to the inverted proportion yields the dividendo property. Componendo is used to simplify equations where sums of terms appear, and it is a standard tool in ICSE Class 10 commercial mathematics for solving problems on ratios, mixtures, and partnership accounts.
steps: Componendo is the algebraic rule that allows adding 1 to both sides of a proportion $a/b = c/d$ to produce the equivalent equation $(a+b)/b = (c+d)/d$.

The derivation relies on three supporting mechanisms: writing the proportion as a fractional equality, adding 1 to both sides, and expressing that 1 as $b/b$ and $d/d$ to combine the terms under a common denominator.
This step requires that denominators $b$ and $d$ are strictly non-zero.
The mechanism initiates with the given proportion $a/b = c/d$.
Adding 1 to both sides gives $a/b + 1 = c/d + 1$.
Converting the integers to fractions matching the denominators yields $a/b + b/b = c/d + d/d$.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “(a+b)/a = (c+d)/c”) reveals the misconception that the sum is divided by the first term instead of the second term — confusing componendo with its counterpart dividendo.
remember: State the componendo property for a proportion a:b = c:d.
Given the proportion 5:7 = 15:21, verify componendo numerically.
A student claims that componendo can be applied to the proportion 0:4 = 0:6. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Dividendo is a property of proportion that states: if four quantities a, b, c…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Dividendo is a property of proportion that states: if four quantities a, b, c, d are in proportion (a/b = c/d), then the ratio of the difference of the first pair to its second term equals the ratio of the difference of the second pair to its second term. Symbolically, (a – b)/b = (c – d)/d. The quantities a, b, c, d must be non‑zero and have the same units so that the ratios are dimensionless. Dividendo is derived by subtracting 1 from each side of the proportion a/b = c/d, giving (a/b) – 1 = (c/d) – 1, which simplifies to (a – b)/b = (c – d)/d. It is the counterpart of componendo (which adds the denominator) and together they lead to the combined componendo‑dividendo rule. Dividendo is used to transform a proportion into a simpler form, often making it easier to solve for an unknown term or to compare ratios. It applies only when the denominators b and d are not zero, and the subtraction does not change the equality because the same operation is performed on both sides of the original proportion.
steps: Let’s walk through dividendo step by step.
You already know that if a/b = c/d, the two fractions are equal.
In the previous node we added the denominator to the numerator (componendo).
Now we do the opposite: subtract the denominator from the numerator.
Start with a/b = c/d.
Subtract 1 from both sides: a/b – 1 = c/d – 1.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “(a – b)/a = (c – d)/c”) reveals the misconception that dividendo subtracts the numerator from the denominator instead of subtracting denominator from numerator, confusing the order of terms.
remember: State the dividendo property for a proportion a:b = c:d, including the necessary condition on the terms.
Given the proportion 5:7 = 15:21, apply dividendo and write the resulting proportion in simplest integer form.
A student writes the dividendo of a/b = c/d as (a‑b)/a = (c‑d)/c. Identify the error and explain why it is incorrect.

cards.title: In a proportion (a)/(b) = (c)/(d) (with b,d ≠ 0)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a proportion (a)/(b) = (c)/(d) (with b,d ≠ 0), alternendo states that the ratio of the first terms equals the ratio of the second terms: (a)/(c) = (b)/(d). This property follows directly from cross‑multiplication: ad = bc ⇒ dividing both sides by cd gives a/c = b/d. Alternendo is one of the classic proportion transformations (along with componendo, dividendo, invertendo) and is used to simplify equations, compare quantities, or derive new proportions without altering the equality. It applies to any four non‑zero quantities in proportion, whether they represent lengths, weights, speeds, or pure numbers. The transformation preserves the proportionality constant, so any subsequent operation (e.g., taking square roots, adding a constant) remains valid on the new proportion.
steps: Alternendo is a rearrangement of the cross-product equality ad = bc, which is the fundamental property of any proportion a/b = c/d.
Step 1 – Recognise the proportion.
A recipe requiring 3 cups of flour for 2 cups of sugar, scaled to 9 cups of flour for 6 cups of sugar, is written as 3/2 = 9/6.
Step 2 – Apply alternendo.
Swap the middle terms to group the flours and the sugars: the ratio of the flours (first terms) equals the ratio of the sugars (second terms), resulting in 3/9 = 2/6.
Both sides simplify to 1/3.
remember: State the alternendo property for the proportion (a)/(b) = (c)/(d).
Given (7)/(x) = (21)/(15), use alternendo to form a new proportion and solve for x.
Evaluate whether the statement “Alternendo can be applied only when all four terms are positive” is true or false. Justify.

cards.title: Invertendo is a property of proportion stating that if four quantities a, b, c…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Invertendo is a property of proportion stating that if four quantities a, b, c, d are in proportion (a: b = c: d), then their reciprocals are also in proportion (b: a = d: c). Formally, from a/b = c/d we obtain b/a = d/c, provided none of the terms is zero. This follows directly from the definition of equality of ratios and the fact that taking reciprocals of equal non‑zero numbers preserves equality. Invertendo is one of the classic “componendo‑dividendo‑alternendo‑invertendo” transformations used to simplify proportion equations. It connects closely with alternendo (a: c = b: d) and with componendo/dividendo, which combine sums and differences of terms. Mastery of invertendo allows a student to rewrite a proportion in a form that isolates the unknown, especially when the unknown appears in the denominator. The property holds for any real numbers (or algebraic expressions) representing lengths, weights, speeds, or any measurable quantities, as long as the terms are non‑zero. In the CISCE ICSE Class 10 syllabus, invertendo is taught after alternendo and before direct applications, forming a toolkit for solving proportion‑based word problems in commercial mathematics such as profit‑loss, partnership, and mixture problems.
steps: Invertendo lets you flip both ratios of a proportion and the equality still holds.
Here is why: if a/b = c/d, then by cross‑multiplication a·d = b·c.
Dividing both sides by a·c (non‑zero) gives d/c = b/a, which is exactly b/a = d/c.
Consider a practical Indian example: a recipe uses 3 kg of flour for every 5 kg of sugar (3:5).
If you have 5 kg of sugar, how much flour?
The proportion is 3/5 = x/5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “a: c = b: d”) reveals confusion with alternendo, which swaps the means instead of inverting each ratio.
remember: State the invertendo property for a proportion a: b = c: d.

cards.title: Direct applications of ratio and proportion involve using the equality of two…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Direct applications of ratio and proportion involve using the equality of two ratios (a: b = c: d) to solve real‑life problems where quantities vary together. The concept builds on the sub‑topics of this chapter: a simple proportion (a/b = c/d), continued proportion (a/b = b/c), mean proportional (b = √(ac)), and the transformation rules componendo, dividendo, alternendo, and invertendo. In a direct application, at least three of the four quantities are known, and the unknown is found by cross‑multiplication (ad = bc). The quantities involved may be lengths (metre, m), time (second, s), mass (kilogram, kg), money (rupee, ₹), or any other measurable entity, but the ratio itself is dimensionless because it compares like units. For example, in a mixture problem the ratio of milk to water (both measured in litres) is used; in a time‑and‑work problem the ratio of work done to time taken (work in arbitrary units, time in seconds) is equated. Thus, direct applications translate the abstract equality of ratios into concrete calculations for mixtures, partnerships, speed‑distance‑time, simple interest, and similar contexts, relying on the foundational properties studied in the sibling nodes.
steps: The core strategy for solving proportion problems is to identify two varying quantities, express their relationship as an equality of two ratios, and solve for the unknown using cross-multiplication.
A ratio compares two quantities (a:b or a/b), and a proportion equates two ratios (a/b = c/d).
Transformation rules like componendo, dividendo, alternendo, and invertendo are algebraic tools used to rewrite proportions into simpler forms, making the unknown easier to isolate.

The systematic method involves: (1) Identifying the two quantities that vary together, (2) Writing the known ratio as a fraction, (3) Setting it equal to the fraction containing the unknown, (4) Cross-multiplying (ad =…
These methods apply directly to Indian contexts such as calculating travel time on railways, sharing partnership profits, or determining interest on savings.
To solve a mixture problem like milk and water in a 3:2 ratio where adding 5L of water changes the ratio to 3:4, represent the original quantities as 3x and 2x.

cards.title: Factorisation of polynomials is the process of expressing a polynomial as a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Factorisation of polynomials is the process of expressing a polynomial as a product of its irreducible factors over the set of real numbers (or integers, as required). The chapter rests on three interconnected theorems. The Factor Theorem states that for a polynomial f(x), (x‑a) is a factor if and only if f(a)=0; thus the zeros of the polynomial correspond exactly to its linear factors. The Remainder Theorem asserts that when f(x) is divided by (x‑a), the remainder is f(a); this provides a rapid evaluation tool without performing long division. Complete factorisation combines these results: by repeatedly applying the Factor Theorem to locate rational zeros (using the Rational Root Theorem) and then dividing out the corresponding linear factors, a polynomial of degree n can be reduced to a product of linear and/or irreducible quadratic factors. Mastery of these ideas enables students to solve polynomial equations, simplify rational expressions, sketch graphs by identifying intercepts, and tackle higher‑order algebraic problems that appear in the ICSE Class 10 examination. The chapter also reinforces the division algorithm for polynomials, synthetic division, and the relationship between coefficients and roots (Vieta’s relations) as a natural extension.
steps: Factorisation simplifies complex polynomials by breaking them into manageable linear or irreducible quadratic components.
The Factor Theorem provides a direct test for these components: if substituting a value 'a' into a polynomial f(x) results in zero, then (x‑a) is a guaranteed factor.
This is supported by the Remainder Theorem, which establishes that the remainder of f(x) divided by (x‑a) is simply f(a), allowing for instant evaluation without the labor of long division.

Complete factorisation leverages these theorems to systematically reduce a polynomial of degree n into its simplest product form, which is essential for solving equations and identifying x-intercepts on a graph.

cards.title: The Factor Theorem is a fundamental result linking the zeros of a polynomial to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Factor Theorem is a fundamental result linking the zeros of a polynomial to its factors. Let f(x) be a polynomial with real coefficients. For any real number a, the theorem states: f(a)=0 (x-a) is a factor of f(x). Equivalently, when f(x) is divided by the linear divisor (x-a), the remainder is f(a) (Remainder Theorem). If that remainder is zero, the divisor is a factor. This creates a two‑way bridge: evaluating the polynomial at a tests factorhood, and knowing a factor gives a root a. The theorem extends to any number of distinct linear factors; a polynomial of degree n can have at most n distinct real zeros, each yielding a factor (x-a_i). It underpins complete factorisation, where a polynomial is expressed as a product of linear and irreducible quadratic factors over the reals. The theorem also connects to the Factor Theorem’s converse: if (x-a) is a factor, then f(a)=0. This duality is used to find unknown coefficients when a factor is given, and to solve polynomial equations by reducing degree step‑by‑step.
steps: The Factor Theorem tells us that a polynomial f(x) has (x-a) as a factor exactly when f(a)=0.
Here is why: dividing f(x) by (x-a) gives quotient q(x) and remainder R; by the division algorithm f(x)=(x-a)q(x)+R.
Substituting x=a yields f(a)=R.
Thus the remainder is the polynomial’s value at a. If f(a)=0, the remainder vanishes and (x-a) divides f(x) evenly — it is a factor.
Conversely, if (x-a) is a factor, the remainder must be zero, so f(a)=0.
This two‑way link lets us test factors without long division: just evaluate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “f(a)=0 means a is a factor”) reveals the misconception that the number a itself is a factor, confusing the root with the factor (x-a).
remember: State the Factor Theorem in your own words.
If f(x)=2x^3-5x^2+3x-1, explain why evaluating f(1) tells you whether (x-1) is a factor.
A student claims that because f(2)=0 for f(x)=x^3-4x^2+5x-2, the polynomial has exactly three linear factors. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The Remainder Theorem states that for any polynomial f(x) with real…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Remainder Theorem states that for any polynomial f(x) with real coefficients and any real number a, when f(x) is divided by the linear divisor (x-a), the remainder is the constant f(a). Formally, there exist a quotient polynomial q(x) and a constant R such that f(x) = (x-a)q(x) + R, and substituting x=a gives f(a)=R. This theorem links polynomial evaluation directly to division, showing that the remainder is independent of the quotient’s degree. It is a direct consequence of the Division Algorithm for polynomials and is the foundation for the Factor Theorem (which is the special case R=0). The theorem holds for any polynomial over a field, and in the ICSE Class 10 syllabus we restrict to real coefficients and real a. It enables quick remainder finding without performing long division, and it underpins synthetic division and complete factorisation techniques taught later.
steps: Let’s walk through the Remainder Theorem step by step, using a familiar Indian context.
Stage 1 – Recall polynomial division.
In Class 9 you divided 2x^3+3x^2-5x+6 by x-2 using long division.
You obtained a quotient and a remainder.
The division algorithm guarantees Dividend = (Divisor)×(Quotient) + Remainder.
The remainder’s degree is always less than the divisor’s degree.
remember: State the Remainder Theorem in your own words and identify the remainder when a polynomial f(x) is divided by (x-a).
Explain why the remainder must be a constant when dividing by a linear polynomial (x-a).
Evaluate the remainder when f(x)=2x^3-5x^2+3x-4 is divided by x-3 using the Remainder Theorem. Show all steps.

cards.title: Complete factorisation of a polynomial f(x) with integer (or rational)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Complete factorisation of a polynomial f(x) with integer (or rational) coefficients is the expression of f(x) as a product of its irreducible factors over the integers (or real numbers). The process relies on the Factor Theorem: if f(a)=0 then (x‑a) is a factor, and the Remainder Theorem: the remainder on dividing f(x) by (x‑a) is f(a). By testing possible rational roots given by the Rational Root Theorem (factors of constant term ÷ factors of leading coefficient), we identify linear factors. Synthetic division or long division reduces the polynomial degree step by step. When the remaining quotient is a quadratic that does not factor further over the integers (discriminant < 0), it is left as an irreducible quadratic factor. The final result is f(x) = k·(x‑r₁)(x‑r₂)…(x‑rₘ)·(quadratic₁)… where k is the leading coefficient and each rᵢ is a rational root. This representation is unique up to ordering of factors.
steps: Let’s factorise f(x) = 2x³ – 3x² – 11x + 6 completely.
Step 1 – List possible rational roots.
Constant term = 6 (factors ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6).
Leading coefficient = 2 (factors ±1, ±2).
Possible roots = ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6, ±½, ±3/2.
Step 2 – Test roots using the Factor Theorem.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing only ±1, ±2, ±4) reveals the misconception that the denominator must be 1, ignoring the leading coefficient’s factors.
remember: State the Rational Root Theorem and list all possible rational roots for the polynomial 3x³ – 5x² + 2x – 4.
Explain why synthetic division can be used only when dividing by a linear factor of the form (x – a) and not by a quadratic divisor.
Evaluate the statement: “If a cubic polynomial has one rational root, the remaining quadratic factor will always factorise further into linear factors with integer coefficients.”.

cards.title: The concept of determining unknown coefficients in a polynomial using the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The concept of determining unknown coefficients in a polynomial using the Factor Theorem builds directly on the Factor Theorem and Remainder Theorem. The Factor Theorem states that for a polynomial P(x), (x-a) is a factor if and only if P(a)=0. When a polynomial contains unknown coefficients (e.g., P(x)=x^3+px^2+qx+6), and we are given that a specific linear binomial (x-a) is a factor, substituting x=a into P(x) yields an equation in the unknown coefficients. If multiple factors are known, each gives an equation, forming a system of linear equations that can be solved simultaneously. This process is an application of the Factor Theorem and relies on the Remainder Theorem, which asserts that the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x-a) is P(a); a zero remainder confirms the factor. Once the coefficients are found, the polynomial can be factorised completely using methods from the previous node (complete factorisation). The relationship between the sub-concepts is hierarchical: the Factor Theorem provides the condition P(a)=0; the Remainder Theorem explains why that condition works; and complete factorisation uses the determined coefficients to break the polynomial into irreducible factors. This node focuses exclusively on the algebraic manipulation required to extract unknown coefficients from given factor information, limited to polynomials of degree up to three (cubic) as per the ICSE Class 10 syllabus.
