Mastery of these interconnections enables solving problems that ask for the equation of a line under mixed conditions (e.g., “passing through a point and parallel to a given line”) and for verifying geometric properties such as collinearity, right angles, or the shape of a quadrilateral formed by intersecting lines.
steps: The slope-intercept form (y = mx + c) and the two-point form (y − y₁) = [(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)] (x − x₁) are two dialects of the same language, both describing the same straight line using different ingredients.
The slope-intercept dialect requires the steepness (m) and the y-intercept (c), similar to a ladder leaning against a wall where m is the climb-to-step ratio and c is the height at the wall.
The two-point dialect requires two landmarks; once the coordinates of two points are known, the slope is fixed, and the line is uniquely determined.
Parallel lines are like railway tracks; they never meet because they possess identical steepness (m₁ = m₂).
To find a parallel line passing through a specific point, copy the slope of the original line and apply the point-slope form.
Perpendicular lines function like a crossroad; their slopes are negative reciprocals, meaning their product is −1 (e.g., 2 and −½).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “y = mx + b where b is the x‑intercept”) reveals the misconception that the constant term always gives the x‑intercept, confusing the roles of intercepts.
remember: Recall: Write the slope‑intercept form of a line and state what each symbol represents.
Reasoning: Two lines have equations 2x + 3y = 6 and 4x + 6y = 12. Are they parallel, coincident, or intersecting? Explain your reasoning.
Evaluate: A student claims that the line through (1, 2) and (3, 6) is perpendicular to the line through (0, 0) and (2, −1). Is the claim correct? Justify.

cards.title: Similarity in geometry describes figures that have the same shape but possibly…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Similarity in geometry describes figures that have the same shape but possibly different sizes. Two triangles are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in proportion. The chapter introduces five interconnected sub‑concepts: (1) Size transformation – a dilation (enlargement or reduction) about a centre with a scale factor k; every length multiplies by k, angles remain unchanged. (2) Congruency comparison – congruent figures are a special case of similar figures where the scale factor is 1; all corresponding sides and angles match exactly. (3) AA (Angle‑Angle) condition – if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the triangles are similar; this follows from the angle‑sum property of triangles. (4) Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) applications – a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally; the converse also holds and is used to prove similarity in many configurations. (5) Areas of similar triangles – the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of corresponding sides (or any corresponding linear dimension). These ideas build a toolkit for solving real‑world scaling problems such as map reading, model making, and indirect height measurement.
steps: The one thing to remember: Similarity lets you replace a difficult measurement with a simple proportion because shape stays constant while size changes.
Here is why: (1) A dilation multiplies every length by the same factor k but leaves angles untouched, so the “shape” is preserved.
(2) Congruence is just similarity with k = 1; knowing this prevents the common error of treating congruent triangles as a separate, unrelated topic.

(3) The AA criterion is the most efficient similarity test — you only need two angles, the third follows automatically from the 180° angle sum. (4) The Basic Proportionality Theorem turns a parallel line into a…
(5) The area‑ratio rule (area₁/area₂ = (side₁/side₂)²) converts a linear scale into an area scale, essential for map‑area calculations.
Consider a Class 10 student standing beside a banyan tree at noon.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Similar triangles are a subset of congruent triangles”) reveals the misconception that similarity is stricter than congruence, reversing the inclusion relationship.

cards.title: A size transformation (also called a dilation) is a mapping of the plane that…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
A size transformation (also called a dilation) is a mapping of the plane that fixes a point O (the centre of dilation) and sends every other point P to a point P′ such that O, P, P′ are collinear and OP′ = k·OP, where k (≠ 0) is the scale factor. If k > 0 the image lies on the same ray OP; if k < 0 it lies on the opposite ray, producing a half‑turn about O. Key properties:
1. Lengths are multiplied by |k|.
2. Angles are preserved (the transformation is conformal).
3. Orientation is preserved for k > 0 and reversed for k < 0.
4. Area of any region is multiplied by k². Two figures related by a size transformation are similar; congruence is the special case |k| = 1. The centre O may be inside, on, or outside the figure. In coordinate geometry, with centre at the origin, the mapping is (x, y) → (kx, ky). This concept underpins the later study of similarity criteria (AA), the Basic Proportionality Theorem, and area ratios of similar triangles.
steps: Dilation is a proportional mapping where every point moves along a ray originating from a fixed centre, ensuring the figure maintains its shape while changing size.
Supporting arguments:
The centre of dilation acts as the origin point for all expansion or contraction vectors.
Because every point moves along a ray from the centre, the relative angles between lines remain constant.
Linear scaling is uniform, meaning every segment length is multiplied by the same constant |k|.
Area scaling is non-linear, increasing by the square of the scale factor because both base and height dimensions are scaled.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing A′ 3 cm beyond A along the ray, or on the opposite side of O) reveals the misconception that the scale factor measures displacement from the original point, or that a positive factor flips the side — the factor scales the…
remember: Define scale factor in a size transformation and state its effect on lengths and angles.
A dilation has centre O and scale factor 2. Point A is 3 cm from O. Where is the image A′? Explain the reasoning.
A student claims: “A dilation with scale factor –1 is exactly the same as a rotation of 180° about the centre.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Congruency comparison distinguishes between congruent figures and similar…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Congruency comparison distinguishes between congruent figures and similar figures. Two triangles are congruent (ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF) when all three corresponding sides are equal in length and all three corresponding angles are equal in measure; the scale factor is exactly 1. The five standard congruence criteria are SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS (right‑angle‑hypotenuse‑side). Two triangles are similar (ΔABC ∼ ΔDEF) when corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in proportion; the scale factor k ≠ 1 in general. Every pair of congruent triangles is automatically similar (k = 1), but the converse is false. This node focuses on recognising which criterion applies, understanding that congruence implies equality of all corresponding linear measurements (perimeter, altitude, median, area) whereas similarity only guarantees proportionality of those measurements. The relationship between the two concepts is foundational for later work on the Basic Proportionality Theorem and area ratios of similar triangles.
steps: Two triangles are either congruent (same size and shape when scaled by k = 1) or similar (same shape and proportional sides when scaled by k ≠ 1). - Size transformations multiply every length by a constant scale factor…
Congruent triangles occur when k = 1, making figures coincide perfectly so all three sides and angles match, tested via SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and RHS shortcuts.
Similar triangles occur when k ≠ 1, maintaining equal corresponding angles and sides in ratio k, tested via AA, SAS, and SSS similarity criteria.
Congruence is simply a special case of similarity where the scale factor equals one, meaning every congruent pair is also similar, but not vice versa.
Consequences differ by scale: congruent triangles share equal perimeters and areas, whereas similar triangles scale perimeters by k and areas by k².
Let us compare two triangles drawn on a notebook page.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “similar triangles are always congruent because they look alike”) reveals the misconception that shape similarity implies size equality, confusing proportionality with equality.

cards.title: The AA (Angle‑Angle) similarity criterion states that if two angles of one…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The AA (Angle‑Angle) similarity criterion states that if two angles of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles of another triangle, then the triangles are similar. Formally, for ΔABC and ΔDEF, if ∠A = ∠D and ∠B = ∠E (or any two corresponding pairs), then ΔABC ~ ΔDEF. Consequently, the third angles are automatically equal (∠C = ∠F) because the angle sum of a triangle is 180°. Similarity implies corresponding sides are in proportion: AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD. This criterion is a direct consequence of the fact that fixing two angles fixes the shape uniquely; size may vary. It is distinct from congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) which require equal corresponding sides as well. AA is the most economical similarity test — only angle measurements are needed, no side lengths. It underpins many geometric proofs, the Basic Proportionality Theorem, and area‑ratio results for similar triangles.
steps: Similar triangles share the same shape but may differ in size, functioning like a photograph and its enlargement, whereas congruent triangles are identical in both shape and size.
The AA criterion serves as the primary shortcut to declare two triangles similar by verifying only two angles.
Step 1 – Why two angles are enough.
The third angles are equal because the sum of interior angles in any triangle is 180°.
If ∠A = ∠D and ∠B = ∠E, then ∠C = 180° – (∠A+∠B) and ∠F = 180° – (∠D+∠E).
Since the summed pairs are equal, ∠C = ∠F must also be equal, fixing the triangle's shape.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer suggests the misconception that the third angle must be measured independently, ignoring the angle-sum property.
remember: State the AA similarity criterion in your own words and explain why the third angles become equal automatically.

cards.title: The Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT), also known as Thales’ theorem, states…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT), also known as Thales’ theorem, states: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides, then it divides those two sides proportionally. In ΔABC, let DE be a line segment with D on AB and E on AC such that DE ∥ BC. Then AD/DB = AE/EC. The converse is equally important: If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then that line is parallel to the third side. Both statements rely on the fact that DE ∥ BC creates two pairs of equal corresponding angles (∠ADE = ∠ABC and ∠AED = ∠ACB), making ΔADE ∼ ΔABC by the AA similarity condition (covered in node). The proportionality of corresponding sides in similar triangles yields AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC, which rearranges to AD/DB = AE/EC. Applications include finding unknown segment lengths, proving lines parallel, and solving real‑world problems like shadow‑height calculations where the sun’s rays act as parallel lines.
steps: Let’s walk through the theorem as if we are drawing it on a notebook.

Sketch a large triangle ABC. Mark a point D on side AB and a point E on side AC. Now draw DE so that it runs parallel to BC. Because DE ∥ BC, the angles at D and E match the angles at B and C respectively (corresponding…
Thus ΔADE and ΔABC have two pairs of equal angles → they are similar by AA. In similar triangles, corresponding sides are in proportion: AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC.
Subtract the numerator from the denominator in the first two ratios: AD/(AD+DB) = AE/(AE+EC).
Cross‑multiplying and simplifying gives AD/DB = AE/EC — the Basic Proportionality Theorem.

Now imagine you only know AD = 3 cm, DB = 6 cm, and AE = 4 cm. You want EC. Write the proportion 3/6 = 4/EC → 1/2 = 4/EC → EC = 8 cm. The converse works the same way: if you measure AD/DB = 2/3 and AE/EC = 2/3, you can…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., EC = 32 m from 24 × 20/15) reveals the misconception of inverting the BPT ratio — AD/DB must equal AE/EC with corresponding sides matched, not crossed.
remember: State the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse in your own words, using a triangle ABC with a line DE parallel to BC.

cards.title: Two triangles are similar when their corresponding angles are equal and their…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Two triangles are similar when their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in proportion. If ΔABC ~ ΔDEF, then AB/DE = BC/EF = CA/FD = k (the scale factor). The Area Theorem for Similar Triangles states: (Area(Δ ABC))/(Area(Δ DEF)) = k^2 Equivalently, the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of any pair of corresponding linear elements — sides, altitudes, medians, angle bisectors, or perimeters. This theorem follows directly from the fact that area of a triangle = ½ × base × height; both base and height scale by k, so area scales by k². The result is dimensionless; areas are measured in square units (cm², m², etc.) while k is a pure number.
steps: The area of two similar triangles scales by the square of their linear ratio, not the ratio itself.
This occurs because area is a two-dimensional product of base and height, both of which are scaled by the same factor k. The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height.
If every linear dimension is multiplied by k, the new area becomes ½ × (k·base) × (k·height), which simplifies to k² × (original area).
Consider an Indian traffic sign (Δ₁) with sides 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm. A similar, larger sign (Δ₂) has a longest side of 100 cm. The scale factor k is 100/50 = 2.
The area of Δ₁ is 600 cm².
The area of Δ₂ is 2² × 600 = 2400 cm².

cards.title: This concept node extends similarity to practical applications: maps, plans…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This concept node extends similarity to practical applications: maps, plans, and scale models. A scale factor k (also called representative fraction) is the ratio of a length on the map/model to the corresponding actual length, both expressed in the same units. If k = (1)/(50000), then 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground. Because similarity preserves shape, all corresponding lengths scale by k, all areas scale by k^2, and volumes (if considered) scale by k^3. The node connects the AA similarity criterion (node 12_004), Basic Proportionality Theorem (node 12_005), and area theorem (node 12_006) to real‑world problems: given a map distance, find the actual distance; given an actual area, find the map area; given a model dimension, find the actual dimension. It also introduces the idea of choosing an appropriate scale so that a large object fits on a standard sheet (e.g., A4 paper) while keeping measurements readable.
steps: Similarity is the foundation for representing large objects on small surfaces, where the ratio of areas equals the square of the ratio of corresponding sides.
Scale factor is the constant ratio between map dimensions and actual dimensions, ensuring geometric consistency.
Length calculations require consistent units before applying the scale factor k. Area calculations must use the square of the scale factor (k^2) because area is a two-dimensional property.
Selecting a scale involves balancing the object's actual dimensions against the available paper size to ensure the drawing fits while remaining legible.
To apply these principles, follow these steps: 1.
Understand the scale: A map scale of 1:20,000 means 1 unit on the map equals 20,000 units on the ground.

cards.title: Similarity in Euclidean geometry is a relation between two figures where one…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Similarity in Euclidean geometry is a relation between two figures where one can be obtained from the other by a size transformation (uniform scaling) possibly combined with rigid motions (translation, rotation, reflection). For triangles, similarity is established by any of the following criteria: 1. AA (Angle‑Angle): two pairs of corresponding angles are equal → the third pair is automatically equal. 2. SSS (Side‑Side‑Side): three pairs of corresponding sides are in proportion. 3. SAS (Side‑Angle‑Side): two pairs of sides are in proportion and the included angles are equal. When triangles are similar with scale factor k (ratio of any pair of corresponding sides), the following hold: - All corresponding linear dimensions (altitudes, medians, perimeters) are in the ratio k. - Areas are in the ratio k². - The Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) states that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally; its converse also holds and is frequently used to prove similarity in exam problems. Congruency is a special case of similarity where k = 1 (identical size and shape). The chapter builds from size transformation (node 12_002) through congruency comparison (12_003), AA conditions (12_004), BPT applications (12_005), to area relations (12_006). This node synthesises those ideas and maps them onto typical CISCE question patterns.
steps: The area of a similar triangle increases by the square of the scale factor, while linear dimensions increase proportionally.

This principle is the foundation for solving all CISCE similarity problems. - The scale factor k acts as a multiplier for all lengths; if ΔABC ~ ΔDEF with k = 2, every side, altitude, and perimeter of ΔABC is twice that…
Area scales by k²; a poster-sized Rangoli requires four times the powder of a postcard version because the area grows by 2² = 4.

CISCE exams categorize similarity into three main types: Proof-type questions requiring BPT or AA, "Find-the-value" problems involving algebraic side expressions, and word problems like shadow-height calculations.

A reliable workflow ensures accuracy: sketch and label the diagram, identify the similarity criterion, write the formal similarity statement (e.g., ΔXYZ ~ ΔUVW), apply the ratio rules, and verify units.
Strategic time management is vital; allocate 5–7 minutes per 4-mark problem and always write the similarity statement explicitly, as it secures partial credit even if arithmetic errors occur.

cards.title: A locus (plural: loci) is the set of all points in a plane that satisfy a given…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A locus (plural: loci) is the set of all points in a plane that satisfy a given geometric condition. In ICSE Class 10 Commercial Mathematics the chapter focuses on two families of conditions. 1. Fixed‑distance loci – From a point: the locus is a circle with the given point as centre and the fixed distance as radius. From a line: the locus consists of two lines parallel to the given line, each at the fixed perpendicular distance on either side. 2. Equidistant loci – From two points: the locus is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the points. From two intersecting lines: the locus is the pair of angle bisectors of the angles formed by the lines. From two parallel lines: the locus is a line parallel to both and midway between them. These loci are not abstract curiosities; they underpin construction problems, optimisation (e.g., locating a warehouse equidistant from two markets), and the geometric reasoning required in later chapters on circles, coordinate geometry, and mensuration. The chapter also introduces the idea of construction using ruler and compass, reinforcing the link between algebraic conditions (distance formulas) and their geometric representations.
steps: Let’s begin with a familiar scene: a cricket field.

The bowler’s crease is a line; the batsman must stay exactly 1.22 m (4 ft) from that line while preparing to bat. Every possible position of the batsman’s front foot forms two lines parallel to the crease, one on each…
That is the locus at a fixed distance from a line.
Now picture a tethered goat tied to a pole with a 5 m rope.
The goat can graze anywhere the rope allows — every point exactly 5 m from the pole.
The boundary of the grazing area is a circle, the locus at a fixed distance from a point.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “locus is the path traced by a moving point” without mentioning the condition reveals the misconception that any motion creates a locus, ignoring the requirement that the motion must obey a specific rule.

cards.title: A locus (plural: loci) is the set of all points in a plane that satisfy a given…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A locus (plural: loci) is the set of all points in a plane that satisfy a given geometric condition. For a fixed distance d from a point P(h, k), the locus is a circle with centre P and radius d; its Cartesian equation is (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=d^2. For a fixed perpendicular distance d from a straight line L: ax+by+c=0, the locus consists of two lines parallel to L at distance d on either side; their equations are ax+by+c=± d√(a^2+b^2). The two sub‑concepts are related: both describe a constant‑distance condition, but the first yields a closed curve (circle) while the second yields an open pair of parallel lines. In coordinate geometry the distance formula √((x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2) and the perpendicular distance formula (|ax_0+by_0+c|)/(√(a^2+b^2)) are the algebraic tools that translate the geometric condition into equations.
steps: The fundamental takeaway is that a locus is the set of all points satisfying a specific geometric condition, which we translate into algebraic equations using distance formulas. - The locus of points at a fixed distance…
The locus of points at a fixed perpendicular distance from a line is a pair of parallel lines, as points can exist on either side of the reference line.
Algebraic translation relies on the distance formula for points and the perpendicular distance formula for lines.
Visualizing these shapes—a closed circle versus two infinite parallel lines—prevents confusion between the two geometric conditions.
Consistent application of the distance formulas ensures that the resulting equations accurately represent the geometric constraints.
To find the locus of points 20 m from a cricket stump at (h,k), we use the distance formula √((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2)=20.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (x+2)^2+(y-3)^2=49) reveals the misconception that the signs transfer directly from the coordinates — the form (x-h) and (y-k) negates them, so -3 appears as +3.

cards.title: The locus of points equidistant from two distinct points A and B is the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The locus of points equidistant from two distinct points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB. Every point P on this line satisfies PA = PB; the line is perpendicular to AB and passes through its midpoint. For two intersecting lines l₁ and l₂, the locus of points equidistant from both lines consists of the two angle bisectors — the internal and external bisectors. Any point P on either bisector has equal perpendicular distances to l₁ and l₂. For two parallel lines l₁ and l₂, the locus is a single line parallel to both and lying exactly halfway between them; every point on this midline has equal perpendicular distance to the two given lines. These three cases exhaust the possibilities for “equidistant from two geometric objects” in plane geometry and are derived from the distance formula and properties of perpendiculars.
steps: The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A(2,3) and B(8,7) is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB. The midpoint M of AB is calculated as ((2+8)/2, (3+7)/2) = (5,5).
The slope of AB is (7-3)/(8-2) = 4/6 = 2/3, so the perpendicular slope is -3/2.
The equation of the line through (5,5) with slope -3/2 is y - 5 = -3/2(x - 5), which simplifies to 3x + 2y = 25.
Algebraic verification using (x-2)²+(y-3)² = (x-8)²+(y-7)² confirms this result.
For intersecting lines y = x and y = -x, the locus consists of the two angle bisectors.
The internal bisector is the x-axis (y=0) and the external bisector is the y-axis (x=0).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3x - 4y - 2 = 0) reveals adding the constants without halving them, i.e. using c1 + c2 rather than (c1 + c2)/2 as the midline constant.
remember: What is the locus of points equidistant from the points A(1,2) and B(5,6).
Explain why the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines consists of two lines, not one.
Evaluate the statement: “The midline between two parallel lines is always closer to the line with the larger constant term.”.

cards.title: The intersection of loci is the set of all points that simultaneously satisfy…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The intersection of loci is the set of all points that simultaneously satisfy two or more given locus conditions. Each individual locus — such as a circle (fixed distance from a point), a pair of parallel lines (fixed distance from a line), a perpendicular bisector (equidistant from two points), or angle bisectors (equidistant from two intersecting lines) — is a geometric figure. Their intersection may consist of zero, one, two, infinitely many points, or even a line segment, depending on the relative positions and parameters. For example, a circle and a line intersect in at most two points; two circles intersect in at most two points; a perpendicular bisector and a circle intersect in at most two points. Solving intersection problems requires identifying each locus from the verbal description, constructing or sketching them accurately, and then determining the common points. This concept extends the basic loci studied in nodes and by combining them to model compound constraints, a key skill for construction and proof questions in the ICSE examination.
steps: Let’s walk through the idea of intersecting loci step by step.
You already know four fundamental loci from the previous nodes: (1) a circle — all points at a fixed distance r from a centre O;
(2) a pair of parallel lines — all points at a fixed distance d from a given line l;
(3) the perpendicular bisector of a segment AB — all points equidistant from A and B;
(4) the angle bisectors of two intersecting lines — all points equidistant from those lines.

Now suppose a problem says: “Find the locus of points that are 4 cm from point O and also equidistant from two intersecting lines l₁ and l₂.” This asks for points that belong to both the circle (centre O, radius 4 cm)…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “2 points because a circle and a line intersect in at most 2 points”) reveals the misconception that the pair of bisectors is treated as a single line, ignoring that there are two separate lines.
remember: What is the maximum number of points in the intersection of a circle and a pair of perpendicular lines (the two angle bisectors of intersecting lines).
A student claims: “If a circle and a line do not intersect, then the distance from the centre of the circle to the line is greater than the radius.” Is this claim correct? Explain.
Evaluate the statement: “The intersection of the perpendicular bisector of segment AB and the circle with centre A and radius AB always consists of exactly two points.”.

cards.title: The locus of a point that moves in a plane such that its distance from a fixed…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The locus of a point that moves in a plane such that its distance from a fixed point (called the focus) is always equal to its perpendicular distance from a fixed straight line (called the directrix) is a parabola. The fixed point F and fixed line d are given; for any point P on the locus, PF = PM where PM is the perpendicular from P to d. The axis of the parabola is the line through F perpendicular to d; the vertex V is the midpoint of the perpendicular from F to d. The distance from V to F (or V to d) is the focal length a. In a coordinate system where the vertex is at the origin, the axis is the x‑axis, and the focus is at (a,0) with directrix x = –a, the equation reduces to y² = 4ax. This concept extends the earlier loci (circle, parallel lines, perpendicular bisector, angle bisectors) by combining a point‑distance condition with a line‑distance condition.
steps: The parabola is the set of all points equally distant from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix).
Here is why: when a point moves so that its distance to the focus equals its perpendicular distance to the directrix, it traces a symmetric curve opening away from the directrix.
Consider a focus F at (a,0) and directrix x = –a.
Take any point P(x,y) on the locus.
The distance PF = √[(x–a)² + y²].
The perpendicular distance from P to the line x = –a is |x + a|.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "a parabola is the set of points equidistant from two fixed points") reveals confusion with the perpendicular bisector locus from node.
remember: State the focus‑directrix definition of a parabola in your own words.
If the focus is at (3,0) and the directrix is x = –3, what is the equation of the parabola.
A student claims that the locus of points equidistant from a point and a line is always a straight line. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The intersection of loci is the set of all points that simultaneously satisfy…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The intersection of loci is the set of all points that simultaneously satisfy two or more given locus conditions. If L₁ and L₂ are the loci for two separate conditions, the required points form the geometric intersection L₁ ∩ L₂. In Euclidean geometry, each basic locus is either a circle (fixed distance from a point), a pair of parallel lines (fixed distance from a line), a perpendicular bisector (equidistant from two points), or an angle bisector (equidistant from two intersecting lines). Their intersections can be found by ruler-and-compass construction or by solving the corresponding equations algebraically. The number of intersection points may be 0, 1, 2, or infinitely many (if the loci coincide). This concept combines the four fundamental loci from earlier nodes to solve compound problems such as “points equidistant from A and B and at a fixed distance from A” or “points at a given distance from a line and also equidistant from two intersecting lines.” It is the bridge between isolated locus constructions and multi‑condition geometric problems that appear in ICSE examinations.
steps: The intersection of two loci is the set of points that satisfy both geometric conditions simultaneously.
You must identify the two conditions, construct each locus independently, locate their crossing points, verify the geometry, and measure the result. 1.
Translate the words: Read the problem to identify the two conditions.
For example, “Points 4 cm from A and equidistant from A and B” translates to a circle with centre A (radius 4 cm) and the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Draw each locus separately: Use a sharp pencil and compass.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “always two points”) reveals the misconception that a line always cuts a circle in two points, ignoring the tangent and no‑intersection cases.
remember: What is the intersection of the locus of points at a fixed distance from a point and the locus of points equidistant from two points.

cards.title: A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition. In earlier nodes we studied single‑condition loci: a fixed distance from a point gives a circle; a fixed distance from a line gives two parallel lines; equidistance from two points gives the perpendicular bisector; equidistance from two intersecting lines gives the angle bisectors. When a point must fulfil two conditions simultaneously, the admissible positions are those points that belong to both individual loci. Hence the required locus is the intersection (common part) of the two loci. Algebraically, if the first condition yields an equation F(x,y)=0 and the second yields G(x,y)=0, the simultaneous locus is the solution set of the system F(x,y)=0 and G(x,y)=0. Geometrically, this intersection may be a finite set of points (e.g., a circle cutting a line in up to two points), a line (two coincident lines), or may be empty if the loci do not meet. This node focuses on intersections of the loci already introduced—circles, lines, perpendicular bisectors, and angle bisectors—so that students learn to combine conditions and solve the resulting equations or construct the common points.
steps: When a point must satisfy two locus conditions simultaneously, its possible positions are exactly the points common to the individual loci.
Here is why: each condition alone restricts the point to a specific geometric set; imposing both conditions means the point must lie in the overlap of those sets.

Consider a point P that must be 3 cm from a fixed point A (so P lies on a circle centred at A with radius 3 cm) and also be equidistant from two intersecting lines L₁ and L₂ (so P lies on one of the angle bisectors of…
The circle and the bisector are drawn on the same plane; their overlap consists of the points where the circle cuts the bisector.
First, recognise the individual loci: write the equation of the circle (x‑a)²+(y‑b)²=r² and the equation of the angle bisector (derived from the condition |distance to L₁| = |distance to L₂|).
Second, set up the system of equations.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "It is the union of the two loci") reveals the misconception that satisfying either condition is enough, confusing intersection with union.
remember: State the meaning of "locus satisfying two conditions simultaneously" in one sentence.
A circle of radius 5 cm centred at (0,0) and a line y=2 are drawn on the same plane. Explain, without solving, why the circle and the line can intersect in at most two points.
Consider two distinct parallel lines L₁: y=1 and L₂: y=4. A student claims that the locus of points equidistant from L₁ and L₂ is a single line. Is the claim correct? Justify.

cards.title: Locus is the collection of all points in a plane that satisfy a given geometric…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Locus is the collection of all points in a plane that satisfy a given geometric condition. The conditions are: (1) a fixed distance r from a given point P → a circle with centre P and radius r; (2) a fixed distance d from a given line l → two lines parallel to l at distance d on either side; (3) equidistant from two distinct points A and B → the perpendicular bisector of segment AB; (4) equidistant from two intersecting lines l₁ and l₂ → the pair of angle bisectors of the angles formed by l₁ and l₂. The synthesis node expects the student to combine these loci, identify their intersections, and translate word problems into algebraic equations using the distance formula or the perpendicular distance from a point to a line. Mastery includes recognising degenerate cases and applying the loci to construction-type questions that appear in the ICSE board paper.
steps: Recall the four elementary loci from previous concept nodes to solve complex problems through systematic integration of coordinate geometry and construction techniques.

A point P(2,3) with a fixed distance of 5 cm forms a circle, a line 3x+4y‑12=0 with a fixed distance of 2 cm forms two parallel lines at 3x+4y‑12=±10, two points A(‑1,2) and B(5,‑4) form a perpendicular bisector passing…
Complex ICSE problems require combining the four elementary loci to find intersection points that simultaneously satisfy multiple distance and position conditions.
Algebraic translation of geometric rules relies on squaring distance equations to eliminate radicals and solving simultaneous systems for coordinates.
Step-by-step construction protocols demand separate sketching of each locus component followed by precise marking of all valid crossing points.
Marking schemes in board examinations allocate specific points for locus identification, equation formulation, intersection calculation, and geometric justification.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the misconception that locus always means a straight line, confusing distance from a point with distance from a line.
remember: What is the locus of points that are at a constant distance r from a fixed point O.
A point P moves so that its perpendicular distance from the line 3x‑4y+12=0 is always 5 units. Write the equations of the two lines that form the locus.
Evaluate the statement: “The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is a single straight line.”.

cards.title: Chapter 14 of ICSE Class 10 Mathematics provides a concise overview of the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Chapter 14 of ICSE Class 10 Mathematics provides a concise overview of the three major families of circle theorems that will be studied in detail later: Angle properties (angles subtended by chords, arcs and tangents at the centre and circumference), Cyclic properties (characteristics of quadrilaterals whose vertices lie on a circle, especially the supplementary nature of opposite angles), and Tangent and secant properties (relationships between a tangent, a secant, the radius and the lengths of intercepts). The overview shows how these families are linked: angle results form the basis for proving cyclic quadrilateral theorems, which in turn lead to the power‑of‑a‑point and alternate‑segment theorems for tangents and secants. By presenting the chapter’s purpose—connecting pure geometry to real‑world objects like wheels, gears, arches and roundabouts—the overview motivates why mastering these properties is essential for solving problems in engineering design, architecture, and everyday measurements.
steps: Circle geometry is defined by three interconnected families of theorems that govern how lines and points interact with a circular boundary.
These properties allow us to calculate hidden dimensions and angles in structures ranging from jewellery bangles to large-scale civil engineering projects.
Angle properties describe how arcs and chords dictate the size of angles at the centre and circumference.
Cyclic properties define the rigid constraints of four-sided figures inscribed within a circle.
Tangent and secant properties explain the mathematical relationship between lines that touch or intersect a circle and the circle’s radius.
These families are logically linked: angle properties provide the foundation for cyclic quadrilateral theorems, which in turn support the derivation of tangent-secant relationships.
remember: Recall the three main subtopics named in the overview of Chapter 14.
Reason why understanding angle properties is a prerequisite for grasping cyclic properties in this chapter.
Evaluate the statement: “All circle theorems needed for ICSE Class 10 can be derived from the tangent‑secant power‑of‑a‑point rule alone.”.

cards.title: In a circle with centre O, let AB be a chord (or arc) and P any point on the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a circle with centre O, let AB be a chord (or arc) and P any point on the remaining part of the circumference. The angle at the centre subtended by arc AB is ∠AOB. The angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc is ∠APB. The fundamental theorem states: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠APB. Consequently, all angles subtended by the same arc (or chord) in the same segment are equal: if P and Q lie on the same segment, then ∠APB = ∠AQB. A special case occurs when AB is a diameter; then the angle in the semicircle ∠APB = 90° for any point P on the circle (Thales’ theorem). These relationships hold for any circle regardless of size, and they form the basis for solving problems involving unknown angles, proving concyclicity, and linking to cyclic quadrilateral properties (covered in the next node).
steps: Let’s start with a familiar picture: a circular rangoli drawn on the floor during Diwali.
The centre is where you place the dot, and the coloured arcs are chords.
Pick any two points A and B on the rim. Draw radii OA and OB – they form the central angle ∠AOB.
Now choose a point P anywhere else on the rim (but not on the minor arc AB).
Join PA and PB; the angle ∠APB is the “view from the circumference”.
Why is ∠AOB twice ∠APB?
remember: In a circle with centre O, chord AB subtends an angle of 40° at a point P on the major arc. What is the measure of ∠AOB.
Points A, B, C lie on a circle with centre O. ∠ACB = 35° and points A, B, C are on the same segment. What is ∠AOB.
A diameter PQ of a circle meets the circumference at R. If ∠PRQ = 90°, what can you conclude about triangle PQR.

cards.title: Cyclic properties describe the invariant angle relationships that hold for any…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Cyclic properties describe the invariant angle relationships that hold for any quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a single circle (a cyclic quadrilateral) and for angles subtended by the same chord at the circumference. 1. Opposite‑angle theorem: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠ A + ∠ C = 180° and ∠ B + ∠ D = 180°. 2. Angles in the same segment: If points P and Q lie on the same arc AB (excluding A,B), then ∠ APB = ∠ AQB. 3. Exterior‑angle theorem: The exterior angle formed by producing one side of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle, e.g. ∠ CBE = ∠ ADC when BC is extended to E. These theorems follow from the fact that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc (proved in the Angle properties node). The cyclic quadrilateral theorem is a direct consequence: the two opposite arcs together form the whole circle (360°), so their half‑angles sum to 180°. The same‑segment theorem arises because both angles subtend the identical arc. All relationships are purely angular; no lengths are required.
steps: Let’s build the cyclic properties step by step, linking back to the angle‑at‑centre theorem you mastered in the previous node.
Step 1 – Visualise the set‑up.
Draw a circle with centre O. Mark four points A,B,C,D on the circumference in order.
Join them to form quadrilateral ABCD.

Also draw radii OA, OB, OC, OD. You now have four central angles: ∠ AOB, ∠ BOC, ∠ COD, ∠ DOA. Their sum is 360° because they complete a full turn around O. Step 2 – Relate central angles to circumference angles.

From the Angle properties node, the angle subtended by arc AB at the circumference (say ∠ ACB) is half of ∠ AOB. Similarly, ∠ ADB = 12 ∠ AOB. So any two angles standing on the same arc AB are equal — this is the angles…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “opposite angles are equal”) reveals the misconception that cyclic quadrilaterals behave like parallelograms, confusing supplementary with equal angles.
remember: State the theorem that relates the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral and give the angle sum for each pair.
In the figure, points A,B,C,D lie on a circle with AB as a chord. ∠ ACB = 40°. What is ∠ ADB? Explain why.
A cyclic quadrilateral WXYZ has ∠ W = 110° and ∠ X = 70°. Can this quadrilateral exist? Justify.

cards.title: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact. The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. A secant is a line that intersects the circle at two distinct points. From an external point P, two tangents PA and PB can be drawn; they are equal in length (PA = PB). The power of a point P with respect to the circle is defined as the square of the tangent length (PT²) or, for a secant through P intersecting the circle at A and B, the product PA·PB. This power is constant for all lines through P. The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment (the angle subtended by the chord in the opposite arc). For two intersecting secants PAB and PCD, the products of their segments are equal: PA·PB = PC·PD. These properties link lengths and angles, enabling solution of problems involving circles, tangents, and secants.
steps: Let’s build the tangent‑secant ideas step by step, connecting them to what you already know from angle and cyclic properties. 1.
Tangent touches at one point – Draw a circle with centre O. Pick a point T on the circumference.
Draw radius OT. Now draw a line through T that just grazes the circle; this line is the tangent.
Because the circle is the set of all points at a fixed distance from O, any other point on the tangent would be farther from O than the radius, so the tangent cannot cut the circle again.
The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent — a fact you can prove by contradiction using the shortest distance from a point to a line. 2.
Two tangents from an outside point – Take a point P outside the circle.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the tangents are unequal because the points of contact are different”) reveals the misconception that the distance from P to the circle depends on the direction, ignoring the symmetry of the circle and the congruence of the right…
remember: State the relationship between the lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle.
A tangent PT and a secant PAB are drawn from an external point P to a circle. If PT = 6 cm and PA = 4 cm, find the length of PB.
In the figure, AB is a chord and AT is a tangent at A. If ∠BAT = 35°, what is the measure of ∠ACB where C is any point on the circle on the opposite side of AB.

cards.title: This concept node focuses on the strategic combination of circle theorems to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This concept node focuses on the strategic combination of circle theorems to solve multi-step geometric problems. It integrates three theorem families: (1) Angle properties — angle at centre is twice angle at circumference, angles in the same segment are equal, angle in a semicircle is 90°; (2) Cyclic properties — opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°, exterior angle equals interior opposite angle; (3) Tangent and secant properties — tangent is perpendicular to radius at point of contact, tangents from an external point are equal in length, tangent-secant theorem (tangent² = product of secant segments), intersecting chords theorem (product of segments of intersecting chords are equal), and alternate segment theorem (angle between tangent and chord equals angle in alternate segment). The node teaches students to scan a diagram, identify which theorems apply at each stage, translate geometric relationships into algebraic equations, and solve sequentially for unknown angles or lengths. It emphasizes logical chaining: a result from one theorem becomes the given for the next. No new theorems are introduced; instead, the node builds fluency in selecting and sequencing the theorems mastered in nodes 002, 003, and 004.
steps: The key to solving complex circle problems is to systematically apply the relevant theorems in sequence, translating geometric clues into algebraic equations.
Here is why: a single diagram often contains several overlapping theorem configurations; missing one link breaks the chain.
Consider a typical ICSE problem: a circle with centre O, diameter AB, tangent at C meeting AB extended at D, and a chord CE. Given ∠CAB = 30°, find ∠BCD.
Step 1: Mark all given information on the diagram — radius OC ⟂ tangent CD, AB is diameter so ∠ACB = 90° (angle in semicircle).
Step 2: Use angle sum in ΔABC: ∠ABC = 180° – 90° – 30° = 60°.
Step 3: Recognise that ∠BCD is the angle between tangent CD and chord CB. By the alternate segment theorem (node 004), ∠BCD = ∠CAB = 30°.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Angle in the same segment theorem”) reveals the misconception that any angle equality involving a chord and a point on the circle is the same theorem, confusing the tangent-chord configuration with the chord-chord configuration.
remember: Which theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment.

cards.title: The alternate segment theorem states that in a circle…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The alternate segment theorem states that in a circle, the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle subtended by the chord in the alternate (opposite) segment. Formally, let a circle have centre O. Let PT be a tangent at point P, and let PQ be a chord. Choose any point R on the circle lying on the side of chord PQ opposite to the tangent PT. Then ∠QPT = ∠PRQ. This theorem links three previously studied concepts: (1) the tangent‑radius perpendicular property (∠OPT = 90°), (2) the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference (∠POQ = 2∠PRQ), and (3) the angle in a semicircle is a right angle. The alternate segment is the region of the circle cut off by chord PQ that does not contain the tangent. The theorem is a direct consequence of the fact that the angle between the tangent and the chord equals the angle in the opposite segment because both are half the measure of the intercepted arc (the arc PQ not containing R). It is used extensively to find unknown angles in circle geometry problems, especially when a tangent and a cyclic quadrilateral appear together.
steps: Let’s build the theorem step by step, connecting what you already know.
Step 1: Recall the tangent.
In the previous node you learned that a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
Draw a circle with centre O. Mark point P on the circumference.
Draw tangent PT so that PT ⟂ OP. Step 2: Add a chord.
From P draw a chord PQ. Now you have ∠QPT — the angle between the tangent PT and the chord PQ. This is the “tangent‑chord angle”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the angle between tangent and chord equals the angle at the centre”) reveals the misconception that the tangent‑chord angle is linked to the central angle rather than the inscribed angle in the far…
remember: State the alternate segment theorem in your own words, clearly naming the tangent, chord, point of contact, and alternate segment.
In the diagram (described in words): Circle with centre O. Tangent at P is line PT. Chord PQ is….
A student claims: “The alternate segment theorem works for any line that touches the circle, even if it cuts the circle at another point.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: This concept node focuses on the integrated application of multiple circle…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This concept node focuses on the integrated application of multiple circle theorems to solve complex geometric problems. It builds on three previously established theorem groups: (1) angle properties — angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc; angles in the same segment are equal; angle in a semicircle is a right angle. (2) cyclic properties — opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary; exterior angle equals interior opposite angle. (3) tangent and secant properties — tangent is perpendicular to radius at point of contact; lengths of tangents from an external point are equal; tangent‑secant theorem (PT² = PA·PB) and intersecting chords theorem (PA·PB = PC·PD). The node teaches students to analyse a given configuration, identify which theorems are relevant, draw auxiliary lines if needed, and set up algebraic equations linking unknown angles or lengths. Emphasis is placed on logical sequencing: first mark known angles using angle properties, then use cyclic quadrilateral relations, finally apply tangent‑secant or chord theorems for lengths. Problems often involve a circle with intersecting chords, a tangent and a secant from an external point, and a cyclic quadrilateral formed by intersection points. The solution pathway requires moving fluidly between angle chasing and length calculations, recognising that angle results can feed into length relations via similar triangles or trigonometric ratios (though trigonometry is not required at this level). This node does not introduce new theorems; it synthesises existing ones into a coherent problem‑solving framework.
steps: The key takeaway: In multi‑theorem circle problems, always start with angle chasing using angle and cyclic properties, then use those angle results to identify similar triangles or apply tangent‑secant/chord theorems…
Here is why: angle theorems give direct relationships that are often easier to spot; once angles are known, triangles become similar, revealing proportional sides that link to length theorems.
Consider a typical ICSE problem: a circle with centre O, a tangent at T, a secant through T meeting the circle again at A and B, and a chord CD intersecting AB at P inside the circle.
First, mark the right angle between radius OT and tangent.
Use the alternate segment theorem to equate angle between tangent and chord TA to angle in the opposite segment (angle TBA).
Then apply cyclic quadrilateral properties if points A, B, C, D are concyclic.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference") reveals confusion between the alternate segment theorem and the angle‑at‑centre theorem, indicating the student cannot distinguish tangent‑chord relations from central‑angle…
remember: State the theorem that relates the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact to the angle in the alternate segment.
In a circle, chord AB and chord CD intersect at P inside the circle. If AP = 5 cm, PB = 3 cm, and CP = 4 cm, find PD. Explain which theorem you used.

cards.title: This node consolidates the three core theorem families of ICSE Class 10…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition:
This node consolidates the three core theorem families of ICSE Class 10 Circles: 1. Angle properties – The angle subtended by an arc at the centre (∠AOB) equals twice the angle subtended at any point on the remaining circumference (∠ACB). Angles in the same segment are equal. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).
2. Cyclic properties – A quadrilateral whose vertices lie on a circle is cyclic. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (sum = 180°). The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
3. Tangent and secant properties – A tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact. From an external point P, the lengths of the two tangents PA and PB are equal. For a secant PAB and tangent PT, the tangent-secant theorem states PT² = PA × PB. The synthesis node shows how these theorems interlock: a problem may require using the angle-at-centre rule to find a cyclic quadrilateral angle, then applying the tangent-secant theorem to compute a length. CISCE exam patterns frequently combine two or three theorems in a single multi-mark question, often with a diagram described in words rather than drawn.
steps: Mastery of circle geometry relies on the consistent application of the three core theorem families: angle properties, cyclic properties, and tangent-secant relationships.

The angle-at-centre rule dictates that the central angle is twice the angle at the circumference; for instance, on a clock face, the angle between the hands at the centre is double the angle formed by a person standing…
Cyclic quadrilaterals follow the supplementary rule, where opposite angles (such as those at 12 and 6 o'clock) must sum to 180°.
Tangents are defined by their perpendicularity to the radius at the point of contact, and tangents drawn from an external point to the same circle are always equal in length.

Complex problems require chaining these rules: first, use the angle-at-centre theorem to find a central angle, then apply cyclic quadrilateral properties to find an interior angle, and finally use the tangent-secant…

Effective exam strategy involves sketching the described figure immediately, labeling all known variables, and allocating time based on marks—typically one minute per mark—to ensure all algebraic steps are verified.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the angles are equal”) reveals the misconception that central and inscribed angles are the same, confusing the angle-at-centre theorem with the “angles in the same segment are equal” theorem.
remember: State the theorem that relates the angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle to the angle subtended by the same arc at any point on the remaining circumference.
In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 70° and ∠C = 110°. Verify whether ABCD can be cyclic and explain the reasoning.

cards.title: Chapter 15 Constructions in the CISCE ICSE Class 10 Mathematics syllabus deals…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Chapter 15 Constructions in the CISCE ICSE Class 10 Mathematics syllabus deals with precise geometric drawing using only an unmarked ruler and a compass. The chapter comprises two major families of constructions. First, drawing tangents to a given circle from an external point: this requires locating the points of contact where the line from the external point meets the circle at right angles to the radius. Second, circumscribing and inscribing circles on triangles and regular hexagons: a circumscribed circle passes through all vertices of the polygon, its centre being the intersection of perpendicular bisectors of the sides; an inscribed circle touches each side, its centre being the intersection of angle bisectors. Both families rely on fundamental properties — equal radii, perpendicular radius‑tangent relationship, concurrency of perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors — and on the ability to construct perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, and parallel lines. Mastery of these constructions enables students to solve locus problems, prove geometric theorems, and tackle practical design tasks such as laying out circular gardens or mechanical parts.
steps: The chapter equips you with two powerful construction toolkits: drawing tangents from an outside point and fitting circles around or inside triangles and regular hexagons.

Here is why: every tangent construction hinges on the fact that the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent; every circumscribed circle uses the concurrency of perpendicular bisectors; every…

Consider a circular garden of radius 4 m and a lamp post 10 m from its centre — you need the exact lines from the lamp that just graze the garden; the construction uses the right‑triangle formed by the centre, the…

For a triangular plot, the circumcentre is found by intersecting the perpendicular bisectors of two sides, giving a circle that passes through all three corners — useful for a sprinkler system covering the whole plot.
The incentre, found by intersecting two angle bisectors, yields a circle touching all three sides — ideal for a circular flower bed that fits exactly inside.

An exam trap: students often confuse the circumcentre of an obtuse triangle (which lies outside) with the incentre (always inside); remembering that the circumcentre is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors, not…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “constructing parallel lines and dividing a segment”) reveals the misconception that the chapter repeats Class 9 basic constructions rather than introducing new families specific to circles and polygons.

cards.title: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact. From any external point P (outside the circle) exactly two tangents PA and PB can be drawn to a circle with centre O and radius r. The segments PA and PB are equal in length. The line OP joins the external point to the centre. The radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent (OA ⟂ PA, OB ⟂ PB). Consequently, triangles OAP and OBP are congruent right‑angled triangles (RHS criterion). The length of each tangent is given by PA = PB = √(OP² – r²). The angle between the two tangents, ∠APB, satisfies sin(∠APB/2) = r / OP. These relationships link the external distance, radius, tangent length, and the included angle, forming the core of construction problems involving tangents from an external point.
steps: The two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length because they form congruent right-angled triangles with the circle's radius and the line connecting the external point to the centre.
Supporting arguments:
The radius is always perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact, creating right-angled triangles.
The hypotenuse (the line from the external point to the centre) is shared by both triangles.
The radii are equal, satisfying the RHS (Right-angle, Hypotenuse, Side) congruence criterion.
This geometric relationship allows for the precise calculation of tangent lengths and angles using the Pythagorean theorem and trigonometry.
cards.misconception: An incorrect answer, such as relying on visual symmetry, fails to provide the necessary geometric proof required for mathematical rigor.
remember: State the theorem that guarantees the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length.
If the radius of a circle is 5 cm and the distance from an external point P to the centre O is 13 cm, find the length of each tangent from P to the circle.
Explain why the construction of tangents using the circle on OP as diameter always yields the correct points of contact.

cards.title: A circumscribed circle (circumcircle) of a polygon is a circle that passes…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A circumscribed circle (circumcircle) of a polygon is a circle that passes through all its vertices. Its centre, the circumcentre, is the point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of the polygon’s sides. For a triangle, the circumcentre is equidistant from the three vertices; the circumradius R satisfies R = (abc)/(4Δ) where a,b,c are side lengths and Δ is the area. An inscribed circle (incircle) of a polygon is a circle tangent to each side. Its centre, the incentre, is the intersection of the internal angle bisectors. For a triangle, the incentre is equidistant from the three sides; the inradius r satisfies r = (Δ)/(s) where s = (a+b+c)/(2) is the semiperimeter. A regular hexagon has all sides equal and all interior angles 120°. Its circumcentre and incentre coincide at the hexagon’s centre. If the side length is a, the circumradius R_hex = a and the inradius r_hex = (√(3))/(2)a. Construction of these circles uses only a straightedge and compass: for a triangle, draw perpendicular bisectors of two sides to locate the circumcentre, then draw the circle through any vertex; draw angle bisectors of two angles to locate the incentre, drop a perpendicular to a side to get the inradius, then draw the incircle. For a regular hexagon, construct the hexagon by stepping off the radius on a circle, then the same centre serves for both circles.
steps: The circumcentre is the unique point equidistant from all three vertices of a triangle, found by locating the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of its sides. - A perpendicular bisector is the locus of points…
The circumradius is the distance from this intersection to any vertex.
The incentre is the unique point equidistant from all three sides, found by intersecting the internal angle bisectors.
The inradius is the perpendicular distance from the incentre to any side.
For a regular hexagon, the centre of the circle used to construct the vertices serves as both the circumcentre and incentre.
To construct the circumcircle, draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides of the triangle; their intersection is the circumcentre.

cards.title: This node covers the construction of a triangle when the following three…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node covers the construction of a triangle when the following three elements are given: (1) the length of the base BC, (2) the base angle ∠B (or ∠C), and (3) either the sum (AB + AC = k) or the difference (|AB – AC| = k) of the other two sides. The construction relies on the locus principle: for a fixed base BC and a constant sum k, the vertex A lies on an ellipse with foci B and C; for a constant difference, A lies on a hyperbola. The practical ruler‑and‑compass method translates this locus into a straight‑edge construction. Sum case (AB + AC = k): 1. Draw base BC of given length. 2. At B, construct ray BX making the given base angle with BC. 3. On BX, cut off BD = k (the given sum). 4. Join D to C. 5. Draw the perpendicular bisector of CD; let it meet BD at A. 6. Join A to C. Triangle ABC is the required triangle. Difference case (AB – AC = k, AB > AC): Steps 1‑2 are same. On BX, cut off BD = k. Join D to C. Draw the perpendicular bisector of CD; let it meet BX (produced if necessary) at A. Join AC. Then AB – AC = BD = k. The construction uses the fact that if A lies on the perpendicular bisector of CD, then AC = AD. Hence AB + AC = AB + AD = BD = k (sum case) or AB – AC = AB – AD = BD = k (difference case). This node builds directly on the perpendicular‑bisector and angle‑construction skills from Class 9 and on the circle‑construction techniques (circumcircle/incircle) covered in nodes and. It does not cover constructions involving vertical angle, altitude, median, or cyclic quadrilaterals — those are reserved for subsequent nodes.
steps: Let’s walk through the sum‑of‑sides construction as if we are drawing it on a notebook.
Stage 1 – Draw the base.
Place your ruler and draw a line segment BC exactly 6 cm long (example value).
Label the endpoints B (left) and C (right).
This is the fixed base of the triangle.

cards.title: Common tangents are straight lines that touch two given circles at exactly one…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Common tangents are straight lines that touch two given circles at exactly one point each. For two circles with centres O_1, O_2 and radii r_1, r_2 (let r_1 ≥ r_2), the distance between centres is d = O_1O_2. - Direct common tangents do not intersect the segment O_1O_2. They exist when d > r_1 - r_2. If d = r_1 - r_2 (internal touching), the two direct tangents coincide into one. - Transverse common tangents intersect the segment O_1O_2 between the circles. They exist when d > r_1 + r_2. If d = r_1 + r_2 (external touching), the two transverse tangents coincide into one at the point of contact. If the circles intersect (r_1 - r_2 < d < r_1 + r_2), only two direct common tangents exist. If one circle lies completely inside the other without touching (d < r_1 - r_2), no common tangent exists. Construction uses auxiliary circles: for direct tangents draw a circle centred at O_1 with radius r_1 - r_2; tangents from O_2 to this auxiliary circle give the direction. For transverse tangents use an auxiliary circle of radius r_1 + r_2. The tangent segments from the centres to the auxiliary circle are parallel to the required common tangents. The length of a direct common tangent segment between points of contact is √(d^2 - (r_1 - r_2)^2); for a transverse common tangent it is √(d^2 - (r_1 + r_2)^2).
steps: The number and type of common tangents depend entirely on the distance between the centres relative to the sum or difference of the radii.

You can determine the existence of these lines by comparing the distance d to the radii r_1 and r_2: if d > r_1 + r_2, you have 4 tangents; if d = r_1 + r_2, you have 3; if r_1 - r_2 < d < r_1 + r_2, you have 2; if d =…

Construct direct common tangents by drawing an auxiliary circle with radius r_1 - r_2 at the larger centre, drawing tangents from the second centre to this circle, and then drawing lines parallel to these tangents…

Construct transverse common tangents by drawing an auxiliary circle with radius r_1 + r_2 at the larger centre, following the same tangent-construction process, and drawing parallels to locate the contact points.
Verify the construction by measuring the tangent segment and comparing it to the calculated length using the Pythagorean formula L = √(d^2 - (r_1 r_2)^2).

cards.title: The circumcircle of a regular hexagon is the unique circle that passes through…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The circumcircle of a regular hexagon is the unique circle that passes through all six vertices of the hexagon. Its centre, called the circumcentre, coincides with the geometric centre of the hexagon. Because a regular hexagon can be divided into six congruent equilateral triangles by joining the centre to each vertex, each central angle measures 60°. Consequently, the triangle formed by two adjacent radii and the included side is equilateral, making the circumradius (R) exactly equal to the side length (a). The construction relies on the fact that the perpendicular bisector of any chord of a circle passes through the centre. Therefore, drawing the perpendicular bisectors of two adjacent sides of the hexagon locates the circumcentre at their intersection. Once the centre O is found, a circle drawn with radius OA (where A is any vertex) will pass through all vertices. This construction also demonstrates that the regular hexagon is cyclic, and its circumcircle is the same as the circle that circumscribes each of the six equilateral triangles.
steps: The circumradius of a regular hexagon is always equal to its side length because the hexagon is composed of six equilateral triangles meeting at the centre. - The central angle of a regular hexagon is 60° (360° divided…
Each triangle formed by the centre and two adjacent vertices has two sides equal to the radius.
Since the included angle is 60°, the base angles must also be 60°, confirming the triangle is equilateral.
Therefore, the distance from the centre to any vertex (the radius) must equal the side length.
The circumcentre is found at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of any two sides, as these lines must pass through the centre of the circle.
To construct the circumcircle:

cards.title: A regular hexagon is a six-sided polygon with all sides equal and all interior…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A regular hexagon is a six-sided polygon with all sides equal and all interior angles equal to 120°. Its circumscribed circle (circumcircle) is the unique circle that passes through all six vertices; its centre is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides (also the intersection of the diagonals). The inscribed circle (incircle) is the unique circle tangent to all six sides; its centre coincides with the circumcentre because the hexagon is regular. The circumradius R equals the side length a. The inradius r (apothem) is the perpendicular distance from the centre to any side, given by r = (√(3))/(2)a. Construction uses only a straightedge and compass: (1) draw a circle of radius a, (2) mark six consecutive arcs of radius a on the circumference to obtain vertices, (3) join vertices to form the hexagon, (4) for the circumcircle, use the original circle; for the incircle, drop a perpendicular from the centre to a side to get r and draw the circle. This construction relies on the fact that a regular hexagon can be partitioned into six equilateral triangles of side a.
steps: Let’s build a regular hexagon and its two circles, just like a master carpenter laying out a hexagonal tile pattern for a floor.
Stage 1: Construct the regular hexagon.
You are given a side length, say a = 4 cm. Open your compass to exactly 4 cm. Draw a circle of radius 4 cm — this will become the circumcircle.
Mark a point A on the circumference.

Without changing the compass width, place the needle on A and cut an arc on the circle to get point B. Repeat: from B cut C, from C cut D, from D cut E, from E cut F, and from F you should return to A. Join…
Because the compass radius equals the circle’s radius, each chord AB, BC, equals the radius, so each triangle OAB, OBC, (where O is the centre) is equilateral.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., R = 2a or R = (a)/(2)) reveals the misconception that the hexagon’s diagonal or apothem is the radius, confusing the circumradius with the distance across flats or the inradius.

cards.title: This node synthesises the two core construction families of Chapter 15…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node synthesises the two core construction families of Chapter 15: (1) drawing tangents from an external point to a given circle, and (2) constructing the incircle and circumcircle of a triangle and of a regular hexagon. The tangent construction uses the fact that the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent; the length of the tangent segment from an external point P to a circle with centre O and radius r is √(OP² − r²). For a triangle with sides a, b, c, semiperimeter s = (a+b+c)/2 and area Δ, the incircle radius r = Δ/s and the circumradius R = abc/(4Δ). A regular hexagon of side a has an incircle radius r = a√3/2 and a circumradius R = a; its side equals the radius of its circumcircle. The node emphasises how CISCE board questions combine these constructions — e.g., “Construct a triangle ABC, draw its incircle, then from an external point draw tangents to that incircle” — and tests the ability to switch between geometric construction and algebraic verification.
steps: The takeaway is that successful CISCE construction requires the seamless integration of precise geometric drawing with algebraic verification using the Pythagorean theorem.
The tangent length is derived from the right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the tangent, and the line from the center to the external point.
Construction accuracy depends on using a sharp pencil and keeping the compass radius fixed during repetitive steps like hexagon marking.
The marking scheme rewards both the visual construction steps and the numerical proof, necessitating a balanced time allocation.
Standardized procedures for incircles (angle bisectors) and circumcircles (perpendicular bisectors) must be applied consistently to avoid common errors.
