cards.title: Unit symbols are internationally agreed abbreviations for physical quantities…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Unit symbols are internationally agreed abbreviations for physical quantities, defined by the International System of Units (SI). Each base quantity (length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, luminous intensity) has a unique symbol (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd). Derived quantities (area, volume, speed, force, energy, power, pressure) are expressed as algebraic combinations of base symbols using multiplication (· or space) and division (/, negative exponents). Rules govern capitalization (symbols named after scientists are capitalised, e.g., N for newton), pluralisation (symbols never take an “s”), spacing (a space between number and symbol, e.g., 5 m), and the use of prefixes (k, M, µ, n) that multiply the unit by powers of ten. The chapter also covers writing units in full (kilometre, milligram) versus symbols (km, mg), and the conventions for compound units such as m s⁻¹ or J mol⁻¹. Mastery ensures that any measurement communicated in examinations, laboratory reports, or real‑world transactions follows a single, unambiguous standard.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every physical quantity has a single, universally accepted symbol, and the rules for writing and combining those symbols are fixed — never improvise.

Here is why: measurements are the language of science, commerce, and daily life; a misplaced capital letter or missing space changes the meaning (e.g., “5 ms” could be read as 5 milliseconds or 5 metre‑seconds).
Consider a recipe that says “200 g flour” — the “g” is lower‑case because gram is not named after a person, while “200 W” for a bulb uses capital “W” honouring James Watt.

When you combine units, you treat symbols like algebraic variables: speed = distance ÷ time → m s⁻¹ (or m/s), force = mass × acceleration → kg m s⁻² = N. Prefixes attach directly to the symbol without a space: kilometre…
In examinations, CISCE expects you to write “10 m s⁻¹” not “10m/s” and to avoid “kgs” or “Km”.
Practice by converting everyday statements — “The car travels 60 kilometres per hour” → “60 km h⁻¹” — and checking each rule.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Kg” or “KG”) reveals the misconception that the first letter of the unit name must always be capitalised, confusing unit symbols with ordinary abbreviations.

cards.title: A unit is a standard quantity used to express a physical measurement.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A unit is a standard quantity used to express a physical measurement. The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base units: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for electric current, kelvin (K) for thermodynamic temperature, mole (mol) for amount of substance, and candela (cd) for luminous intensity. Each base unit has a unit symbol (always a single letter or a combination of letters) and a unit name (written in full). Rules for writing units in full and as symbols: 1. Unit names are written in lower case (e.g., metre, newton) except at the start of a sentence. 2. Unit symbols are written in lower case unless the unit is named after a scientist, in which case the first letter is capitalised (e.g., N for newton, Pa for pascal, °C for degree Celsius). 3. Symbols are never pluralised (e.g., 5 m, not 5 ms). 4. No full stop follows a symbol unless it ends a sentence. 5. A space separates the numerical value from the symbol (e.g., 25 kg, not 25kg). 6. Compound units use a centre dot (·) or a space for multiplication (e.g., N·m or N m) and a solidus (/) or negative exponent for division (e.g., m/s or m s⁻¹). These conventions ensure universal readability of scientific data across languages and regions.
steps: The International System of Units (SI) provides the universal language for scientific measurement, replacing informal local units with precise, agreed-upon standards.
Seven base units form the measurement alphabet: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and candela (cd).

Only the kilogram contains a prefix in its name; its symbol is kg, never kG. Naming rules distinguish between words and symbols: Unit names are common nouns (metre, newton) written in lower case unless they begin a…
Symbols are shorthand; if a unit honours a scientist, the first letter is capitalised (e.g., N for Newton, Pa for Pascal, J for Joule), while the second letter remains lower case.
Spacing ensures numerical clarity: A thin space must always separate the number from the symbol (e.g., 25 kg, not 25kg).
Symbols are invariant: Symbols never take an ‘s’ for pluralisation.

cards.title: The rules for combining unit symbols govern how SI base and derived unit…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The rules for combining unit symbols govern how SI base and derived unit symbols are assembled to represent compound physical quantities. Multiplication of units is indicated either by a space (e.g., m s) or a centred dot (·) (e.g., m·s); concatenation without a separator (e.g., ms) is forbidden because it creates ambiguity with prefixed units such as millisecond (ms). Division is shown with a solidus (/) (e.g., m/s) or, preferably in formal work, by negative exponents (e.g., m·s⁻¹). Powers apply to the unit symbol alone (e.g., m², s⁻²) and the exponent follows the symbol directly without a space. SI prefixes (k, M, µ, etc.) are attached directly to the unit symbol with no space or hyphen (e.g., km, µs). Unit symbols are never pluralised (e.g., 5 kg, not 5 kgs) and are not followed by a period except at the end of a sentence. These conventions ensure unambiguous communication of measurements across scientific, commercial, and engineering contexts.
steps: Glue unit symbols together using specific placement rules when a compound physical quantity requires more than one unit.

The core principle is that symbols combine with explicit separators to prevent misinterpretation, requiring a space or centred dot for multiplication, negative exponents or solidi for division, direct prefix attachment…
Multiplication requires a space or centred dot between symbols, such as m·m or m m for area (simplified to m²), because omitting the separator creates a prefixed unit like mm (millimetre).
Division uses a solidus or negative exponent, such as m/s or m·s⁻¹ for speed, because negative exponents avoid stacked fractions and prevent confusion with prefixed units like ms⁻¹.
Powers attach directly as superscripts to the unit symbol without spaces or baseline numbers, ensuring expressions like m² and s⁻² are unambiguous.
Prefixes and pluralization follow strict invariance rules, attaching directly without spaces or hyphens (e.g., km, ms) while refusing plural "s" suffixes (e.g., 5 kg, not 5 kgs).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “N = kg m/s²” without the dot or using “kgm/s²”) reveals the misconception that concatenation without a separator is acceptable — it creates ambiguity with prefixed units and violates the multiplication rule.

cards.title: SI prefixes are standardized symbols that represent integer powers of ten…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: SI prefixes are standardized symbols that represent integer powers of ten, attached to base or derived unit symbols to form decimal multiples and submultiples. Each prefix has a unique name (e.g., kilo, mega, milli, micro) and a single‑letter or two‑letter symbol (k, M, m, µ). The prefix symbol is placed directly before the unit symbol with no space (e.g., km, mg, µs). Prefixes follow strict capitalization rules: those representing 10⁶ and above use uppercase (M, G, T), while those below 10³ use lowercase (k, h, da, d, c, m, µ, n, p, f). The prefix “kilo” (k) is the only lowercase prefix for a positive power. Combining prefixes is forbidden (e.g., “millikilogram” is invalid); instead, use a single appropriate prefix. The numerical value of a measurement changes by the factor 10ⁿ where n is the exponent of the prefix. This system ensures universal readability and avoids ambiguity in scientific, commercial, and everyday contexts.
steps: The one thing to remember: every SI prefix is a shorthand for a power of ten, and it must be glued to the unit symbol without a space, following exact capitalization.

Here is why: the International System of Units (SI) defines 20 prefixes so that any measurement can be expressed compactly, whether it is the wavelength of light (nanometres) or the distance between cities (kilometres).

First, learn the prefix table: quetta (Q, 10³⁰), ronna (R, 10²⁷), yotta (Y, 10²⁴), zetta (Z, 10²¹), exa (E, 10¹⁸), peta (P, 10¹⁵), tera (T, 10¹²), giga (G, 10⁹), mega (M, 10⁶), kilo (k, 10³), hecto (h, 10²), deca (da…
Notice the pattern: large prefixes use uppercase, small ones lowercase, except kilo (k).

Second, practice conversion: to change 5 km to metres, multiply by 10³ → 5 000 m. To change 250 mg to grams, divide by 10³ → 0.25 g. Third, apply the attachment rule: write “ms” for millisecond, not “m s”; write “MHz”…
Fourth, avoid double prefixes: never write “µµF”; use “pF”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing “mc” for micro) reveals the misconception that prefix symbols can be invented from the name’s first letters rather than using the standardized symbol.

cards.title: Derived units are SI units defined as algebraic combinations of the seven base…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Derived units are SI units defined as algebraic combinations of the seven base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela). Each derived unit represents a physical quantity such as force, energy, power, pressure, electric charge, or magnetic flux. The SI assigns special names and symbols to 22 derived units (e.g., newton (N) for force, joule (J) for energy, watt (W) for power, pascal (Pa) for pressure, coulomb (C) for charge, volt (V) for potential difference, ohm (Ω) for resistance). These special symbols are always written with an initial capital letter when named after a scientist (N, J, W, Pa, C, V, Ω) and in lower case otherwise (e.g., Hz for hertz). Derived units can also be expressed purely in base‑unit symbols using multiplication (·) or division (/) and negative exponents (e.g., N = kg·m·s⁻², J = kg·m²·s⁻², W = kg·m²·s⁻³). The rules for writing unit symbols — no plural ‘s’, no full stop, space between multiplied units, solidus or negative exponent for division — apply equally to derived units. Understanding derived units links the abstract base units to measurable quantities in commerce, engineering, and daily life (e.g., electricity tariffs in kWh, tyre pressure in kPa).
steps: Derived units are algebraic combinations of base units that represent physical quantities, with the SI system providing special names and symbols for 22 of these combinations.
Derived units are formed by multiplying or dividing base units according to physical laws (e.g., Force = mass × acceleration).
Special names and symbols are assigned to these combinations to simplify scientific communication (e.g., the newton for force).
Standardized writing conventions ensure clarity, such as capitalizing symbols named after scientists and avoiding pluralization.
These units bridge the gap between abstract base measurements and practical applications like electricity billing and engineering specifications.
To determine a derived unit, apply the physical formula using base units.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing newton, joule and watt as basic units) reveals the misconception that special names replace base units entirely, missing that each is only a shorthand for a fixed base-unit combination.

cards.title: This node covers the internationally agreed conventions for writing SI unit…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node covers the internationally agreed conventions for writing SI unit symbols, as prescribed by the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM) and adopted in the CISCE ICSE Commercial Mathematics curriculum. The conventions ensure unambiguous communication of measurements across languages and disciplines. Key rules include: (1) Unit symbols are printed in roman (upright) type, not italic. (2) Symbols derived from proper names (e.g., newton N, joule J, watt W) start with a capital letter; all others are lower case (e.g., m, kg, s). (3) Symbols are never pluralised — “5 kg” not “5 kgs”. (4) No period (full stop) follows a symbol unless it ends a sentence. (5) A space (preferably a thin space) separates the numerical value from the unit symbol (e.g., “25 °C”, not “25°C”). (6) Compound unit symbols use a centre dot (·) or a space for multiplication (e.g., “N·m” or “N m”) and a solidus (/) or negative exponent for division (e.g., “m/s” or “m·s⁻¹”). (7) Only one solidus is used per expression; parentheses avoid ambiguity (e.g., “J/(mol·K)”). (8) Prefix symbols attach directly to the unit symbol without space (e.g., “km”, “ms”). These conventions apply to all scientific, commercial, and everyday measurements in the ICSE syllabus.
steps: Standardized unit symbols ensure that a scientist in Mumbai, a trader in Delhi, and an engineer in Bengaluru all interpret a measurement identically.
Symbols are mathematical entities, not abbreviations: They do not follow English grammar rules for plurals or punctuation.
Case sensitivity is mandatory: Symbols derived from proper names are capitalized, while others are lower case.
Spacing defines the relationship between values and units: A space acts as a delimiter between the magnitude and the unit.
Compound units require specific operators: Multiplication and division must be clearly demarcated to prevent misreading.
Prefixes are integral to the unit: They modify the unit directly without separation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “5 kgs” or “5kg.”) reveals the misconception that unit symbols follow ordinary English pluralisation and punctuation rules, treating them as abbreviations rather than mathematical symbols.

cards.title: Unit symbols in commercial mathematics are standardised notations that…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Unit symbols in commercial mathematics are standardised notations that represent physical or monetary quantities concisely. The Indian rupee is denoted by ₹ (never “Rs” or “INR” in symbolic work), mass by kg, length by m, time by a (annum) or yr, and percentage by %. Compound units follow algebraic rules: multiplication is shown by a centre dot (·) or space (e.g., ₹·kg⁻¹ or ₹/kg), division by a solidus (/) or negative exponent (e.g., km·h⁻¹). Prefixes (k, M, µ) attach directly to the unit symbol without a space (km, Mg). In commercial contexts, rates such as interest ( % p.a. ), tax ( % GST ), and price ( ₹/unit ) must keep the unit symbol attached to the number with a thin space (e.g., 18 % not 18%). Dimensional consistency requires that every term in an equation carries compatible units; for instance, simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time yields units of ₹ when Rate is in % p.a. (treated as dimensionless fraction) and Time in years. This node extends the rules from and to the specific conventions used in GST invoices, banking, and share trading, ensuring that unit symbols behave as algebraic entities that cancel, combine, and convert correctly.
steps: Correct use of unit symbols in commercial mathematics ensures that every calculation — from GST to compound interest — is dimensionally consistent and universally understood.
First, unit symbols act as algebraic quantities: they multiply, divide, and cancel exactly like numbers, so ₹/kg × kg = ₹.
Second, commercial conventions dictate specific symbols: ₹ for rupees, % for percent, p.a. for per annum, and these must be spaced correctly (e.g., 12 % GST, 8 % p.a.).
Third, mixing abbreviations (“Rs”, “pa”, “kgs”) with symbols breaks the algebraic behaviour and leads to marking penalties.
Consider a GST invoice: a shirt marked ₹800 attracts 12 % GST. Write the rate as 12 % (not 12 percent).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Rs/kg” or “rupees/kg”) reveals the misconception that abbreviations like “Rs” are acceptable in symbolic work — they are not, because only the official symbol ₹ behaves algebraically in equations.

cards.title: Unit symbols are the internationally agreed abbreviations for physical…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Unit symbols are the internationally agreed abbreviations for physical quantities (e.g., m for metre, kg for kilogram, s for second). The International System of Units (SI) prescribes: 1. Writing units in full – the name is written in lower case (metre, kilogram) unless it derives from a proper noun (newton, pascal), in which case the symbol is capitalised (N, Pa) but the full name remains lower case. 2. Symbols – are printed in roman (upright) type, never italicised, and are not followed by a period except at the end of a sentence. 3. Combining unit symbols – multiplication is indicated by a centre dot (·) or a space (e.g., N·m or N m for newton metre); division uses a solidus (/) or negative exponent (e.g., m/s or m·s⁻¹). Only one solidus may appear; parentheses are used for clarity when needed (e.g., J/(kg·K)). 4. Prefixes – are attached directly to the unit symbol without a space (e.g., km, ms, µA). Compound prefixes are forbidden (no µµF). These conventions ensure dimensional consistency, avoid ambiguity, and are mandatory in CISCE examinations and scientific communication.

Second, check if the expression involves multiplication or division; if multiplying, insert a centre dot; if dividing, ensure only one solidus is used or convert to negative exponents.
Third, verify that any prefixes are attached directly to the unit without spaces.
Finally, review the entire expression against the rule that symbols are never italicised and never end in a period unless the sentence does.

cards.title: A turning force is a force that tends to rotate a body about a fixed point…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A turning force is a force that tends to rotate a body about a fixed point called the pivot or fulcrum. Unlike a linear force that produces translation, a turning force produces rotation. The turning effect depends on two factors: the magnitude of the force and the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. This perpendicular distance is often called the moment arm. When the line of action passes through the pivot, the turning effect is zero. The sense of rotation is described as clockwise or anticlockwise. The quantitative measure of a turning force is the moment of force (torque), defined as the product of the force and the perpendicular distance. Turning forces are central to understanding levers, gears, and any device that uses rotation to multiply effort. They also underlie the conditions for rotational equilibrium, where the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
steps: Let’s start with something you do every day – opening a door.
When you push the handle, the door rotates about its hinges.
The hinges are the pivot.
Your push is the force.
Notice that if you push at the handle (far from the hinges) the door swings easily, but if you push near the hinges you must push much harder to get the same swing.
Why?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “a force that moves an object in a straight line” reveals the misconception that any force produces translation only, confusing linear force with turning force.

cards.title: The moment of a force quantifies rotational effectiveness as the product of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The moment of a force quantifies rotational effectiveness as the product of force magnitude and perpendicular distance from the pivot, defined by τ = F × d. This vector quantity uses the SI unit newton-metre (N ), with clockwise moments treated as negative and anticlockwise as positive following the right-hand rule. A force passing directly through the pivot produces zero moment because its perpendicular distance is zero. Furthermore, the principle of moments states that for a rigid body in rotational equilibrium, the algebraic sum of all moments about any point equals zero (Σ τ = 0). This concept builds directly upon the foundational idea of turning forces from earlier lessons and establishes the necessary groundwork for the rotational equilibrium conditions in subsequent nodes.
steps: Moment magnitude is determined by both the size of the applied force and the length of the lever arm from the pivot.
A small force with a long lever arm can produce the same rotational effect as a large force with a short lever arm. This principle explains the mechanical advantage of tools like levers and spanners.
Multiple forces combine through algebraic addition of their individual moments.
Calculating these rotational effects requires a systematic procedure.
Step 1 – Identify the pivot by choosing the exact point around which rotation occurs, such as a hinge, a nail, or the centre of a wheel.
Step 2 – Draw the line of action by extending the force vector infinitely in both directions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer confusing this with joules or impulse stems from mistaking torque for work or force-time products.

cards.title: Equilibrium in mechanics means a body experiences no net force and no net…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Equilibrium in mechanics means a body experiences no net force and no net moment (turning effect). For a rigid body under a system of coplanar forces, two conditions must hold simultaneously: 1. Translational equilibrium – the vector sum of all forces is zero: Σ F = 0. This ensures the centre of mass does not accelerate. 2. Rotational equilibrium – the algebraic sum of moments about any point is zero: Σ M = 0. By the principle of moments, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about the chosen pivot. If only forces act (no couples), satisfying Σ F_x = 0, Σ F_y = 0 and Σ M = 0 guarantees complete equilibrium. A body in equilibrium may be at rest (static equilibrium) or moving with constant velocity (dynamic equilibrium). The concept links directly to moment of a force (node) because moments are the rotational counterpart of forces, and to turning forces (node) which produce those moments. Understanding equilibrium is essential before studying uniform circular motion (node) where a net centripetal force exists but the body is not in translational equilibrium.
steps: Equilibrium requires both translational and rotational balance, meaning the vector sum of forces and the algebraic sum of moments about any point must equal zero.

A complete equilibrium state relies on four supporting arguments: first, forces dictate translational acceleration; second, moments determine rotational turning; third, the choice of pivot simplifies calculations…
Step 1 – Recall forces and moments.

In earlier classes you learned that a force can push or pull a body, and a moment (torque) can turn it. The moment of a force about a point is M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line…
Clockwise moments are taken as negative, anticlockwise as positive (or vice‑versa, but stay consistent).
Step 2 – Translational equilibrium.

cards.title: Uniform circular motion (UCM) is the motion of a particle along a circular path…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniform circular motion (UCM) is the motion of a particle along a circular path of constant radius r with a constant speed v. Because the direction of the velocity vector changes continuously, the particle experiences a centripetal acceleration a_c directed radially inward, of magnitude a_c = (v^2)/(r) = ω^2 r where ω (omega) is the angular speed (rad s⁻¹). The net force required to produce this acceleration is the centripetal force F_c = m a_c = (m v^2)/(r) = m ω^2 r with m the mass of the particle. The period T (time for one revolution) and frequency f (revolutions per second) are related by T = (2π)/(ω), f = (1)/(T) = (ω)/(2π) In UCM the tangential speed is constant, but the velocity vector is not; therefore a continuous inward force is essential. This concept links the turning forces and equilibrium studied earlier (nodes 001‑003) to the work‑energy ideas that follow (node 005).
steps: Uniform circular motion requires a continuous inward force because the direction of the velocity vector changes at every instant, even if the speed remains constant.
The velocity vector is always tangent to the circular path; as the object moves, this tangent rotates, creating a change in velocity that points toward the center.
Newton’s second law dictates that this change in velocity requires a net force, known as the centripetal force, directed radially inward.

In physical systems, this force is provided by specific interactions: tension in a string for a whirling stone, friction for a car on a flat road, or motor torque for a ceiling fan. UCM is not a state of equilibrium…
To analyze this motion, consider a stone tied to a string moving in a circle of radius r with speed v. As the stone moves through a small angle Δθ, the velocity vector changes by Δv.
In the limit where the time interval Δt approaches zero, the ratio Δv/Δt defines the centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “acceleration is tangent to the path because the particle moves forward”) reveals the misconception that acceleration follows the direction of motion, confusing speed change with direction change.
remember: Define uniform circular motion and state the direction of the acceleration of a particle undergoing it.

cards.title: Work is a scalar quantity defined as the product of the magnitude of a constant…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work is a scalar quantity defined as the product of the magnitude of a constant force F acting on a body and the displacement s of the point of application of that force in the direction of the force. Mathematically, W = F · s = F s θ, where θ is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector. The SI unit of work is the joule (J), equivalent to one newton‑metre (N·m). Work can be positive (force component along displacement), negative (force component opposite to displacement), or zero (force perpendicular to displacement or no displacement). Work done by a variable force is obtained by integrating F · ds along the path. Work is the mechanism by which energy is transferred from one system to another; it links directly to the concepts of kinetic energy, potential energy, and power (covered in later nodes).
steps: Work is the physical transfer of energy that occurs only when a force causes displacement in its direction. - A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion, but it only transfers energy (does work) if the…
The angle θ between the force and displacement determines how much of that force is actually contributing to the movement.
Work is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude and sign but no direction, representing the amount of energy transferred.
The sign of the work (positive, negative, or zero) indicates whether energy is being added to or removed from the system.
To determine work, first identify the force and the displacement.
If you push a book across a table, the book moves, so the push transfers energy to the book; work is done.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “watt” or “newton”) reveals confusion between work, power, and force — students often mix the unit of energy (joule) with the unit of power (watt) or force (newton).
remember: State the SI unit of work and write its symbol.
A force of 50 N acts on a box at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. The box moves 4 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the force.

cards.title: Energy is the capacity of a physical system to do work.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy is the capacity of a physical system to do work. It is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J) in the SI system, where 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m²·s⁻². Energy exists in various forms — kinetic (due to motion), potential (due to position or configuration), chemical, electrical, nuclear, etc. — but the total energy of an isolated system remains constant (principle of conservation of energy). Work done on a system equals the change in its energy (work‑energy theorem: W = ΔE). Kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is K = ½ m v². Gravitational potential energy near Earth’s surface is U = m g h, where g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² (often taken as 10 m s⁻² in ICSE problems). Elastic potential energy stored in a spring of constant k compressed or stretched by x is Uₑ = ½ k x². Power is the rate of energy transfer (P = E/t). Machines act as force multipliers, allowing a smaller effort to overcome a larger load, but they cannot create energy; the work output never exceeds the work input (ideal machine: load × load‑distance = effort × effort‑distance).
steps: Total mechanical energy remains constant in an idealized system because work done by gravity converts directly between kinetic and potential forms.
Energy is a scalar quantity measured in joules, quantified via formulas such as K = (1)/(2)mv^2 and U = mgh, and governed by the work-energy theorem (W = Δ E).
Mechanical energy transforms continuously in dynamic systems such as pendulums and rolling objects.
Machines transform energy rather than creating it, adhering strictly to the conservation principle. 1.
Energy is a scalar quantity measured in joules that defines a system's capacity to do work.
remember: State the SI unit of energy and define one joule in terms of newton and metre.

cards.title: Power is the rate at which work is performed or energy is transferred.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Power is the rate at which work is performed or energy is transferred. If a constant force F moves an object through a displacement s in time t, the work done is W = F·s (when force and displacement are parallel). Power P is then P = W/t. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹. Because work equals the change in kinetic or potential energy (ΔE), power also equals the rate of energy change: P = ΔE/t. For a body moving with constant velocity v under a constant force F in the direction of motion, instantaneous power can be written P = F·v. Power is a scalar quantity; it has magnitude but no direction. In the CISCE ICSE curriculum, power links the concepts of work (node) and energy (node) and prepares students for the study of energy forms (node) and machines (nodes‑010).
steps: Power is defined by how quickly work is performed, building upon the understanding that work is force applied over a distance and energy is the capacity to do that work. - The rate of work determines power: if two…
To determine power, first calculate the work done against gravity (W = mgh) or against resistance (W = F·s).
Then, divide the total work by the time taken (t) to find the average power in watts.
If force and velocity are provided, use the product P = F·v.
Finally, ensure all units are in SI (joules for work, seconds for time) before calculating the final power value.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “power is measured in joules”) reveals the misconception that power and work are the same quantity, confusing energy amount with energy rate.
remember: Define power and state its SI unit.
A force of 50 N pushes a box at a constant velocity of 2 m s⁻¹. Calculate the power delivered by the force.

cards.title: Energy is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J) that quantifies the capacity…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J) that quantifies the capacity of a system to perform work. In Class 10 Physics we classify energy into several types: 1. Mechanical energy – the sum of kinetic energy (KE = ½ m v²) and gravitational potential energy (PE = m g h). 2. Chemical energy – stored in molecular bonds; released during reactions (e.g., fuels, food). 3. Electrical energy – carried by moving charges; powers circuits and lightning. 4. Nuclear energy – released from changes in atomic nuclei (fission/fusion). 5. Thermal (heat) energy – internal kinetic energy of particles; often a by‑product of other conversions. All these forms obey the principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one type to another. The SI unit for every form is the joule (J = kg·m²·s⁻²). Power (P = W/t) describes how fast energy is transferred, linking the concepts of work (W = F·s·cosθ) and energy. Understanding the inter‑conversion among these types is essential for analysing machines, circuits, and natural phenomena.
steps: Let’s start from what you already know: work is done when a force moves an object, and power tells how quickly that work happens.
Energy is the “currency” that makes work possible.
Stage 1 – Mechanical energy.
Imagine a stone of mass m held at height h above the ground.
It has gravitational potential energy PE = m g h because gravity can do work on it when released.
As it falls, PE decreases while kinetic energy KE = ½ m v² increases.
cards.misconception: This misconception often arises from not recognising thermal energy as a legitimate form.

cards.title: Load (L) is the resistive force that a simple machine is designed to overcome…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Load (L) is the resistive force that a simple machine is designed to overcome or support, measured in newtons (N) in the SI system, and it is directly proportional to effort for a given mechanical advantage. The load acts at the load arm, which is the perpendicular distance from the fulcrum to the line of action of the load. A machine multiplies the applied effort (E) to balance or move a larger load, and the ratio of load to effort defines the mechanical advantage (MA) as: MA = (L)/(E) In an ideal, frictionless machine, the velocity ratio (VR) equals the MA, whereas real machines use efficiency ( ) to relate the two through: = (MA)/(VR) × 100\% Understanding load is essential before analysing effort and the principle of conservation of energy in machines. This concept connects to the moment of a force (node) because the turning effect of the load about the fulcrum must be balanced by the effort's moment for equilibrium.
steps: The turning effect of a force about a pivot is the moment of a force (node), where clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal when a machine is in equilibrium.

The load is the weight or resistance placed on one side of a simple lever's fulcrum, while the effort is the force applied on the opposite side. - The output resistance in every simple machine is the load, which the…
The actual mechanical advantage falls slightly below the ideal velocity ratio due to friction at the fulcrum and contact surfaces consuming energy.
A crowbar lifting a heavy paving stone demonstrates this balance, where the stone is the load and the push on the long end is the effort.
The next node quantifies effort and shows how to choose the effort arm length to achieve a desired mechanical advantage.

cards.title: Effort (symbol E) is the external force applied to a machine to overcome a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Effort (symbol E) is the external force applied to a machine to overcome a resisting load (symbol L). In the context of simple machines — levers, pulleys, inclined planes, wheel‑and‑axle, wedge, screw — effort is the input force that the user supplies. Its SI unit is the newton (N). The mechanical advantage (MA) of a machine is defined as the ratio of load to effort: MA = L / E. Consequently, effort can be expressed as E = L / MA. The velocity ratio (VR) is the ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load: VR = d_E / d_L. For an ideal (frictionless) machine, MA = VR; for real machines, efficiency η = (MA / VR) × 100 %. Effort, load, MA, VR and efficiency are inter‑related; knowing any three allows calculation of the fourth. Effort is a vector quantity — its direction matters — and is always applied at the effort arm of the machine. The concept builds on the earlier understanding of force, work and energy, and it is essential for analysing how machines multiply force.
steps: Effort is the input force you supply to a machine, and its primary purpose is to make the task of overcoming a load easier or more convenient.
The relationship E = L / MA demonstrates that increasing mechanical advantage directly reduces the effort required.
Efficiency acts as a bridge between ideal theoretical performance and the reality of energy dissipation due to friction.
Directional control is a key function of effort, as seen in fixed pulleys where the magnitude of force remains constant but the application becomes more ergonomic.
The velocity ratio dictates the trade-off between the distance the effort moves and the distance the load moves. 1.

cards.title: The principle of conservation of energy states that in an isolated system the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The principle of conservation of energy states that in an isolated system the total energy remains constant over time. Energy may change form — kinetic, potential, chemical, electrical, thermal — but the sum of all forms before any process equals the sum after the process. Mathematically, E_initial = E_final or Δ E = 0. This principle links the concepts of work (energy transfer by force), power (rate of energy transfer), and machines (devices that transform energy while ideally conserving it). In real systems non‑conservative forces such as friction convert mechanical energy into heat, so the mechanical energy alone is not conserved, but the total energy including thermal form still obeys the law. The principle underpins the analysis of pendulums, roller coasters, hydroelectric dams, and all machines studied in this chapter.
steps: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, serving as the unifying principle for all work and energy transformations.
Energy is conserved across all physical interactions, meaning the total energy of a closed system remains invariant regardless of internal changes.
Mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) is perfectly conserved only in the absence of non-conservative forces like friction or air resistance.
Real-world systems dissipate mechanical energy into heat and sound, but the total energy accounting remains balanced.
The law provides a rigorous method for calculating system states by equating initial and final energy totals.
To apply this, consider a cricket ball thrown upward.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Energy is always conserved in every part of a machine”) reveals the misconception that mechanical energy alone is conserved in real systems, ignoring conversion to heat or sound.
remember: State the principle of conservation of energy in your own words.
A simple pendulum swings back and forth. Explain why it eventually comes to rest even though energy is conserved.
