cards.title: Modern Physics in Class 10 ICSE introduces the behaviour of atomic nuclei.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Modern Physics in Class 10 ICSE introduces the behaviour of atomic nuclei. Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus, emitting α‑particles (He nuclei), β‑particles (electrons or positrons) and γ‑rays (high‑energy photons). Each emission changes the proton number (Z) and mass number (A) according to well‑defined rules: α‑decay reduces Z by 2 and A by 4; β‑decay changes Z by ±1 while A stays constant; γ‑decay leaves both unchanged but lowers nuclear energy. Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (e.g., U‑235) into two lighter fragments plus neutrons and ≈200 MeV energy per fission. Nuclear fusion is the combining of light nuclei (e.g., H‑2 + H‑3 → He‑4 + n) releasing ≈17.6 MeV. Both processes obey Einstein’s mass‑energy equivalence E = Δ m c^2. The chapter links these phenomena to real‑world applications: radiocarbon dating, medical tracers, nuclear reactors, and the Sun’s energy. It also stresses safety: ionising radiation can damage living tissue, so shielding, distance and time limits are essential.
steps: Radioactivity, fission, and fusion are fundamental nuclear processes that demonstrate how matter can be converted into energy to power our world and advance medicine. - Radioactivity allows unstable nuclei to reach…
Nuclear fission releases energy by splitting heavy, unstable nuclei into smaller fragments, a process used in commercial power reactors.
Nuclear fusion releases energy by combining light nuclei, which is the primary energy source for stars like the Sun.
Mass-energy equivalence explains that the energy released in these reactions comes from a tiny loss in total mass.
These nuclear phenomena are essential for practical applications, including carbon dating, medical imaging, and electricity generation.

The process begins with radioactivity, where an unstable nucleus like radium-226 ejects an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons) to become radon-222, represented by the equation _88^226Ra → _86^222Rn + _2^4α.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the mass number should stay 210”) reveals the misconception that α‑emission does not change the mass number, confusing it with γ‑decay where A is unchanged.
remember: A student writes the nuclear equation for α‑decay of polonium‑210 as _84^210Po → _82^206Pb + _2^4α. Identify whether the equation is correct and justify your answer.
Explain why β⁻‑decay increases the atomic number by one while the mass number remains the same, using the transformation of a neutron inside the nucleus.
A sample of carbon‑14 (half‑life 5730 years) is found to have 25 % of its original activity. Estimate the age of the sample and show the reasoning.

cards.title: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable atomic nucleus…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of an unstable atomic nucleus accompanied by the emission of ionising radiation. Three primary radiations exist: alpha (α) – a helium nucleus (2 p + 2 n), charge +2e, mass ≈ 4 u; beta (β⁻) – a high‑speed electron (charge −e, negligible mass) emitted when a neutron converts to a proton; gamma (γ) – high‑frequency electromagnetic photons (no charge, no mass) released when an excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state. Each decay changes the parent nucleus into a daughter nucleus, altering the proton number (Z) and/or mass number (A) according to conservation laws. The decay constant λ (s⁻¹) gives the probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay. Activity A (becquerel, Bq) = λN, where N is the number of undecayed nuclei. Half‑life T½ = ln 2 / λ is the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay. The decay law N = N₀e^(−λt) describes the exponential decrease of N with time t. Nuclear equations balance both mass number and atomic number (e.g., ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He). SI units: activity – becquerel (Bq = 1 decay s⁻¹); half‑life – second (s); decay constant – s⁻¹.
steps: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of particles or energy from an unstable nucleus, governed by a constant probability of decay per nucleus per second.

Here is why: first, the nucleus seeks a more stable configuration; if the neutron‑to‑proton ratio is too high, a neutron converts to a proton emitting a β⁻ particle, while if the nucleus is too heavy it ejects an α…

Second, after α or β emission the daughter nucleus may be left in an excited state; it then releases the excess energy as a γ photon without changing Z or A. Third, the decay of each nucleus is independent and random…

Fourth, half‑life T½ = ln 2 / λ provides a convenient measure: after one half‑life half the original nuclei remain, after two half‑lives a quarter, and so on. Fifth, activity A = λN tells how many decays occur per…

Consider a sample of ¹³¹I (half‑life 8 days) used in thyroid therapy: initially its activity is high, but after 24 days (three half‑lives) only 1/8 of the original nuclei remain, reducing the dose to the patient.

In Indian hospitals, technetium‑99m (half‑life 6 h) is generated on‑site because its short half‑life means it cannot be transported far. An exam trap: students often think γ decay changes the element; it does not — only…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “curie is the SI unit”) reveals the misconception that the older non‑SI unit curie (3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq) is still the standard, confusing historical usage with current SI definition.
remember: What is the SI unit of radioactive activity and how is it defined.
A nucleus of ²²⁶₈₈Ra undergoes α decay. Write the balanced nuclear equation and name the daughter nucleus.
Evaluate the statement: “Gamma radiation is the most penetrating because it has the highest energy.”.

cards.title: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy, unstable nucleus
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy, unstable nucleus (e.g., U‑235 or Pu‑239) into two lighter fragments plus a few neutrons and a large amount of energy. The reaction is triggered when a neutron is captured, making the nucleus oscillate and split. The mass of the products is slightly less than the original mass; the missing mass Δm is converted to energy E = Δm c² (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei (e.g., ¹H, ²H, ³H) to form a heavier nucleus (e.g., ⁴He). Because the binding energy per nucleon rises sharply up to iron, the fused nucleus has lower total mass than the reactants; the mass defect again appears as energy via E = Δm c². Both processes obey conservation of nucleon number (A) and charge (Z). In fission, a chain reaction can be sustained if each split releases ≥1 neutron that causes another split; critical mass and moderator control the rate. In fusion, extremely high temperature (≈10⁷ K) and pressure are needed to overcome Coulomb repulsion; the Sun’s core achieves this gravitationally. The energy released per reaction is ~200 MeV for typical fission and ~17.6 MeV for the D‑T fusion reaction. Applications: fission in nuclear power reactors and atomic bombs; fusion in hydrogen bombs and experimental reactors (tokamaks, laser‑inertial confinement).
steps: Nuclear fission and fusion are large-scale nuclear transformations that release energy by converting mass defect into kinetic energy, obeying the conservation of nucleon number and charge.
Fission occurs because heavy nuclei, such as uranium-235, are unstable and can lower their total energy by splitting into lighter fragments.
Fusion occurs because light nuclei, such as deuterium and tritium, have low binding energy per nucleon and release energy when merging into a more stable helium-4 nucleus.
Both processes are governed by the mass-energy equivalence principle, E = Δm c².
The process of fission is sustained through a chain reaction where neutrons released from one split trigger subsequent splits in nearby nuclei.

To maintain this, a critical mass of fuel is required to prevent excessive neutron leakage, and a moderator is used to slow down fast neutrons, increasing their probability of being captured by fissile nuclei.

A student claims that “fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission because the mass defect is larger.” Evaluate this claim using binding‑energy‑per‑nucleon….
In a reactor, each U‑235 fission releases on average 2.5….

cards.title: Nuclear energy is the energy released when the nucleus of an atom undergoes a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Nuclear energy is the energy released when the nucleus of an atom undergoes a change such as fission (splitting) or fusion (combining). The fundamental principle is Einstein's mass‑energy equivalence, E = mc², where a small loss of mass (Δm) appears as a large quantity of energy because the speed of light c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s is squared. In fission, a heavy nucleus (e.g., U‑235) absorbs a neutron and splits into two lighter fragments plus a few neutrons; the total mass of the products is less than the original mass, and the mass defect Δm is converted to kinetic energy of the fragments and radiation. In fusion, light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen isotopes) combine to form a heavier nucleus; again the product mass is less than the sum of the reactants, releasing energy. A self‑sustaining chain reaction occurs when each fission event releases neutrons that trigger further fissions. The multiplication factor k (average number of neutrons from one fission that cause another fission) must be kept at 1 for steady power; control rods absorb excess neutrons to maintain k = 1. A nuclear reactor core contains fuel (fissile material), moderator (slows neutrons), control rods (absorb neutrons), and coolant (removes heat). The heat generated produces steam to drive turbines for electricity. This node connects the mass‑energy concept to practical energy generation and introduces reactor physics basics.
steps: Mass and energy are interchangeable forms of the same physical reality, governed by the relationship E = mc².
The square of the speed of light (c² ≈ 9×10¹⁶ m²/s²) acts as a massive conversion factor, meaning even a milligram of mass can release enough energy to power a home for years.
In a fission reaction, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the original U‑235 and neutron; this missing mass, or mass defect, is converted directly into energy.
A single fission event of U‑235 typically releases about 200 MeV of energy.
To sustain power, a chain reaction is required where at least one neutron from each fission triggers another, represented by a multiplication factor k = 1.
Control rods, typically made of boron or cadmium, are used to absorb excess neutrons to keep k at 1, while a moderator slows down fast neutrons to increase the probability of further fission.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "E = mc" or using grams for mass) reveals the misconception that the speed of light is not squared or that non‑SI units can be used directly without conversion — both lead to numerically incorrect energy values.
remember: State Einstein's mass‑energy equivalence equation and name each symbol with its SI unit.
Why does a small mass loss in nuclear fission produce a large amount of energy.
A student says: "Nuclear fusion releases more energy per kilogram than fission because the mass defect is larger." Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A nuclear fission reactor is a device that sustains a controlled chain reaction…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A nuclear fission reactor is a device that sustains a controlled chain reaction of neutron-induced fission in fissile material (typically U‑235 or Pu‑239) to produce thermal energy for electricity generation. The core contains fuel assemblies, a moderator (light water, heavy water, or graphite) to slow fast neutrons to thermal energies where fission cross‑sections are high, control rods (boron, cadmium, hafnium) to absorb neutrons and regulate reactivity, and a coolant (water, heavy water, gas, or liquid metal) to transfer heat to a steam generator or directly to a turbine. The mass defect Δm between initial nucleus plus neutron and final fission fragments appears as kinetic energy of fragments, promptly released as heat. The energy released per fission is ~200 MeV (3.2×10⁻¹¹ J). Reactor power P = (energy per fission) × (fission rate). Safety systems include emergency core cooling, containment building, and shutdown rods. Criticality condition: k_eff = 1 (neutron production = loss). Subcritical (k<1) shuts down; supercritical (k>1) increases power. Indian PHWRs (Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors) use natural uranium fuel, heavy water moderator and coolant; LWRs (Light Water Reactors) use enriched uranium and light water.
steps: Nuclear reactors generate safe, steady electricity by harnessing controlled uranium fission to produce steam that drives a turbine.
First, a neutron splits a U-235 nucleus, releasing heat and 2-3 new neutrons that sustain a vital chain reaction.
Second, moderators like heavy water slow these neutrons down because slow thermal neutrons are far more effective at causing further fission.
Third, control rods of boron or cadmium act like a finger on a domino line, absorbing extra neutrons to regulate the reaction rate safely.
Fourth, coolant carries the extreme heat to steam generators, turning water into high-pressure steam that spins turbines and generators to produce power.
Finally, multiple safety systems—including scram rods, emergency cooling, and thick concrete containment structures—guarantee operational safety.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "control rods moderate neutrons") reveals the misconception that control rods slow neutrons — confusing them with the moderator, which is a separate material (water, heavy water, graphite) that reduces neutron kinetic energy without…

cards.title: A nuclear reactor is a device that sustains a controlled fission chain reaction…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A nuclear reactor is a device that sustains a controlled fission chain reaction to produce thermal energy, which is then converted into electrical energy. The core contains fissile fuel (typically U‑235 or Pu‑239) arranged in fuel rods. A moderator (light water, heavy water, or graphite) slows fast neutrons to thermal energies where fission probability is high. Control rods (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons to regulate the reaction rate. Coolant (water, heavy water, CO₂, or liquid sodium) removes heat from the core and transfers it to a heat exchanger, producing steam for a turbine‑generator set. The multiplication factor k must be kept at 1 for steady‑state operation; k>1 leads to power rise, k<1 to shutdown. Energy released per fission ≈ 200 MeV, arising from the mass defect Δm via E=Δm c². Reactors are classified by neutron spectrum (thermal, fast), coolant, and moderator. Safety systems include emergency core cooling, containment, and shutdown rods. The concept links the mass‑energy equivalence (E=mc²) to practical power generation.
steps: The core principle of a nuclear reactor is the controlled release of energy through a self-sustaining fission chain reaction.
This process is governed by the interaction of fuel, moderators, and control mechanisms to maintain a steady energy output.
The reactor pressure vessel houses fuel rods containing ceramic pellets of enriched uranium dioxide, where U-235 nuclei split upon absorbing thermal neutrons, releasing energy and fast neutrons.
Moderators, such as heavy water in Indian PHWRs or ordinary water in LWRs, are essential to slow down fast neutrons so they can trigger further fission events.
Control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials like boron carbide or cadmium regulate the reaction rate by maintaining the multiplication factor k at exactly 1.
Coolant systems remove the generated heat to produce steam, which drives a turbine-generator set, mirroring the energy conversion process of a coal-fired plant.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the moderator absorbs neutrons to control the reaction”) reveals the misconception that moderation and absorption are the same — confusing the role of moderator with that of control rods.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the moderator in a thermal nuclear reactor.
Explain why the multiplication factor k must be kept exactly at 1 for steady‑state power operation.
A reactor uses 3 kg of U‑235 fuel.….

cards.title: A thermal nuclear reactor harnesses a controlled chain reaction of uranium‑235…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A thermal nuclear reactor harnesses a controlled chain reaction of uranium‑235 fission. The core contains fuel rods (enriched U‑235), a moderator (heavy water or graphite) that slows fast neutrons to thermal energies where the fission cross‑section is largest, control rods (boron, cadmium) that absorb neutrons to regulate the reaction rate, a coolant (light water, heavy water, or gas) that removes heat to produce steam, and thick concrete shielding that absorbs escaping radiation. Criticality (k = 1) is maintained by adjusting control‑rod depth. Radioisotopes produced in reactors or cyclotrons find wide application: carbon‑14 (half‑life 5730 years) dates organic artefacts; iodine‑131 (half‑life 8 days) treats thyroid disorders; technetium‑99m (half‑life 6 hours) is the workhorse of diagnostic imaging; cobalt‑60 (half‑life 5.27 years) sterilises medical equipment and food. The energy released per fission follows Einstein’s mass‑energy equivalence, E = Δm c², where the mass defect Δm appears as kinetic energy of fission fragments, neutrons, and gamma photons. Fusion, the merging of light nuclei, promises even greater energy per unit mass but remains experimental for power generation.
steps: Nuclear reactors sustain a controlled chain reaction by ensuring that neutrons released from uranium-235 fission trigger exactly one subsequent fission event.

This process is managed through specific engineering controls that regulate neutron speed and population. - The moderator slows down fast neutrons to "thermal" speeds (approx. 0.025 eV), which significantly increases…
Control rods, composed of neutron-absorbing materials like boron or cadmium, regulate the reaction rate by being inserted or withdrawn to maintain the multiplication factor (k) at exactly 1.
The coolant circulates through the core to extract the thermal energy generated by fission, which is then used to drive steam turbines for electricity generation.
Thick concrete and steel shielding are essential to contain radiation and protect personnel from escaping neutrons and gamma rays.
Radioisotopes serve critical roles in society: Carbon-14 dating measures the decay of organic matter to determine age;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the moderator cools the core”) reveals the misconception that moderator and coolant are the same — confusing neutron economy with heat removal.

cards.title: This synthesis node integrates the core concepts of Chapter 06…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: This synthesis node integrates the core concepts of Chapter 06 — radioactivity (α, β, γ emission), changes in the nucleus (transmutation, decay series), nuclear fission (splitting of heavy nuclei with neutron release) and nuclear fusion (combining light nuclei with enormous energy release) — into a coherent framework for CISCE ICSE Class 10 Physics examination preparation. It explicitly links the half-life decay law N = N_0 (1/2)^t/T_1/2 and the mass-energy equivalence E = Δ m c^2 to the typical question patterns: short-answer definitions, balanced nuclear equations, numerical problems on activity, half-life, mass defect and binding energy, and descriptive questions comparing fission and fusion. The node also maps the marking scheme (1-mark recall, 2-mark reasoning, 3-mark numerical, 4-mark evaluation) and highlights the examiner’s emphasis on correct SI units, proper notation (e.g., ^A_ZX), and logical step-by-step presentation. By consolidating the content from concept nodes 002 and 003 and adding exam-oriented practice, this node enables a student to move from isolated facts to applied problem-solving and critical evaluation, which is the expected cognitive demand of the board paper.
steps: Success in the CISCE physics exam depends on mastering the relationship between nuclear stability and energy release, supported by precise mathematical application.

The core takeaway is that nuclear reactions are governed by the conservation of mass number (A) and atomic number (Z), while energy release is dictated by the conversion of mass defect into kinetic energy.
Supporting arguments:
Radioactive decay is a statistical process where the half-life remains constant regardless of the sample size, following an exponential decay pattern.
Nuclear fission and fusion are fundamentally different: fission splits heavy nuclei to achieve stability, while fusion merges light nuclei to reach a more tightly bound state.
The mass-energy equivalence E = Δ m c^2 is the universal bridge between the "missing mass" in a reaction and the energy released.
